What is claimed is:

1. A charging control system for a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch, the system comprising:

a plurality of connector stations, each connector station of the plurality comprising a contactor connected between the electrical branch and a respective electric-vehicle connector of the plurality of electric-vehicle connectors, a connector current sensor arranged to measure a connector current of the respective electric-vehicle connector, and a control-pilot interface arranged to present an assigned limit to a vehicle coupled to the respective electric-vehicle connector;

a branch current sensor arranged to measure a branch current of the electrical branch upstream of the contactors of the plurality of connector stations;

an isolated local bus; and

a controller coupled to the plurality of connector stations and to the branch current sensor over the isolated local bus, the controller configured to store a branch limit that is lower than a sum of ratings of the plurality of electric-vehicle connectors and to store, for each active connector of the plurality of electric-vehicle connectors, a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value;

wherein the controller is configured to, at each allocation interval:

subtract, from the branch limit, a measured non-charging branch load of the electrical branch and a configurable safety reserve, to obtain an available charging current;

assign the minimum sustaining current to those sessions of the active connectors that can receive the minimum sustaining current from the available charging current, and then distribute a remaining portion of the available charging current among the active connectors according to the energy-deficit values;

send each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector station; and

verify a resulting connector current of that connector station with the connector current sensor of that connector station; and

wherein the controller is further configured to, when the measured branch current remains above the branch limit after a reduced pilot command has been sent and a verification interval has elapsed, open the contactors of the plurality of connector stations one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch limit.

2. The system of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured to obtain the measured non-charging branch load as a difference between the measured branch current and a sum of the connector currents measured by the connector current sensors of the plurality of connector stations.

3. The system of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured not to reclose a contactor that has been opened in the stored shedding order until the connector current sensor of the connector station of that contactor reports zero connector current, the control-pilot interface of that connector station reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.

4. The system of claim 3, wherein the controller is configured to draw the randomized recovery delay for each contactor independently from a configured range, whereby contactors opened together in the stored shedding order do not reclose in unison.

5. The system of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured to record a welded-contactor condition for a connector station when the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector station remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector station.

6. The system of claim 5, further comprising a local fault indicator, wherein the controller is configured, upon recording the welded-contactor condition, to inhibit the contactors of the other connector stations supplied by the electrical branch and to operate the local fault indicator.

7. The system of claim 1, further comprising a network interface and a nonvolatile memory, wherein the controller is configured to receive remote schedules and authorizations through the network interface, to store a signed local authorization token and a last accepted branch limit in the nonvolatile memory, and, during a network outage, to continue already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and subject to opening the contactors in the stored shedding order when the measured branch current remains above the last accepted branch limit.

8. The system of claim 7, wherein the controller is configured not to start a session at a newly connected electric-vehicle connector during the network outage unless the signed local authorization token authorizes that electric-vehicle connector and has not expired.

9. The system of claim 7, wherein the controller is configured to append meter records to a tamper-evident local sequence in the nonvolatile memory, each meter record being appended together with a value computed over that meter record and over a preceding entry of the tamper-evident local sequence, and to upload the appended meter records through the network interface when communication returns.

10. The system of claim 1, further comprising a service input, wherein the controller is configured, in response to the service input, to associate local connector identifiers with the contactors of the plurality of connector stations by commanding one low-energy pilot transition at a time through the control-pilot interface of a commanded connector station and confirming a response at the connector current sensor of that connector station, and to store an association between a local connector identifier and a contactor only after the connector current sensor that responds to the commanded low-energy pilot transition agrees with the commanded connector station.

11. The system of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured to assign no current at the allocation interval to a session of an active connector for which the remaining available charging current is less than the minimum sustaining current of that active connector, rather than to assign to that session a current below its minimum sustaining current.

12. The system of claim 11, wherein, when the available charging current is insufficient for every session of the active connectors to receive its minimum sustaining current, the controller is configured to select the sessions to which the minimum sustaining current is assigned in order of the energy-deficit values.

13. The system of claim 1, wherein to verify the resulting connector current the controller is configured to compare the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of a connector station with the assigned limit sent to that connector station and, when the measured connector current exceeds that assigned limit, to use the measured connector current rather than that assigned limit as the load of that connector station at a next allocation interval.

14. The system of claim 1, wherein the electrical branch is polyphase, the branch current sensor comprises a transducer for each phase conductor of the electrical branch, and the controller is configured to take as the measured branch current the greatest of the per-phase current magnitudes reported by the transducers.

15. A method of controlling charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch having a branch limit that is lower than a sum of ratings of the plurality of electric-vehicle connectors, each electric-vehicle connector of the plurality being served by a contactor, by a connector current sensor, and by a control-pilot interface, and the electrical branch having a branch current sensor upstream of the contactors, the method comprising:

storing, for each active connector of the plurality of electric-vehicle connectors, a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value;

at each allocation interval, subtracting from the branch limit a measured non-charging branch load of the electrical branch and a configurable safety reserve, to obtain an available charging current;

assigning the minimum sustaining current to those sessions of the active connectors that can receive the minimum sustaining current from the available charging current, and then distributing a remaining portion of the available charging current among the active connectors according to the energy-deficit values;

sending each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding electric-vehicle connector and verifying a resulting connector current with the connector current sensor of that electric-vehicle connector;

sending a reduced pilot command when a measured branch current from the branch current sensor is above the branch limit; and

when the measured branch current remains above the branch limit after the reduced pilot command has been sent and a verification interval has elapsed, opening the contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch limit.

16. The method of claim 15, further comprising obtaining the measured non-charging branch load as a difference between the measured branch current and a sum of the connector currents measured by the connector current sensors of the plurality of electric-vehicle connectors.

17. The method of claim 15, further comprising withholding reclosure of a contactor opened in the stored shedding order until the connector current sensor of the electric-vehicle connector of that contactor reports zero connector current, the control-pilot interface of that electric-vehicle connector reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.

18. The method of claim 15, further comprising recording a welded-contactor condition for an electric-vehicle connector when the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that electric-vehicle connector remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that electric-vehicle connector, and, upon recording the welded-contactor condition, inhibiting the contactors of the other electric-vehicle connectors supplied by the electrical branch and operating a local fault indicator.

19. The method of claim 15, further comprising storing a signed local authorization token and a last accepted branch limit in a nonvolatile memory, and, during a network outage, continuing already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and declining to start a session at a newly connected electric-vehicle connector unless the signed local authorization token authorizes that electric-vehicle connector and has not expired.

20. A non-transitory computer-readable medium storing instructions that, when executed by a processing circuit of a controller coupled over an isolated local bus to a plurality of connector stations supplied by a common electrical branch and to a branch current sensor arranged to measure a branch current of the electrical branch upstream of contactors of the plurality of connector stations, each connector station comprising one of the contactors, a connector current sensor, and a control-pilot interface, cause the controller to:

store a branch limit that is lower than a sum of ratings of the electric-vehicle connectors served by the plurality of connector stations, and store, for each active connector, a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value;

at each allocation interval, subtract from the branch limit a measured non-charging branch load of the electrical branch and a configurable safety reserve, to obtain an available charging current;

assign the minimum sustaining current to those sessions of the active connectors that can receive the minimum sustaining current from the available charging current, and then distribute a remaining portion of the available charging current among the active connectors according to the energy-deficit values;

send each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector station and verify a resulting connector current with the connector current sensor of that connector station; and

when a measured branch current from the branch current sensor remains above the branch limit after a reduced pilot command has been sent and a verification interval has elapsed, open the contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch limit.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part of this disclosure and show particular embodiments by way of illustration. Other embodiments may be used and structural or logical changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views.

Overview of the system

FIG. 1 shows a charging control system in which an edge controller 100 manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch. A branch conductor 102 supplies the plurality of connectors from a single point of protection. The allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, referred to in this description as the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors that the branch conductor 102 supplies. The branch limit is a stored value that corresponds to the aggregate current the branch is permitted to carry, and may be derived from the rating of the protective device of the branch, from a site limit imposed by the supplying utility or by an energy management authority, or from both.

The branch conductor 102 supplies a first connector station 110 and a second connector station 112. Two connector stations are shown for clarity of illustration. The system accommodates a larger plurality of connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each further connector station of the plurality. The branch conductor 102 also supplies a non-charging load 114, which represents lighting, building services, and other equipment that is connected to the same branch and that is not under the control of the edge controller 100.

A branch current sensor 104 measures total current on the branch conductor 102 upstream of the contactors of the connector stations. Because the branch current sensor 104 is located upstream of those contactors, the current it measures includes both the current drawn by the connector stations and the current drawn by the non-charging load 114. The branch current sensor 104 may be a current transformer, a Rogowski coil, a Hall-effect sensor, a shunt with an isolated amplifier, or another transducer that reports the magnitude of alternating current on a conductor. Where the branch is polyphase, the branch current sensor 104 comprises a transducer for each phase conductor of the branch, and measured branch current is taken as the greatest of the per-phase magnitudes, so that the branch limit governs the most heavily loaded phase.

The edge controller 100 communicates with the connector stations over an isolated local bus 106. The isolated local bus 106 carries assigned current limits and contactor commands from the edge controller 100 to the connector stations, and carries connector current measurements and control-pilot status from the connector stations to the edge controller 100. The isolated local bus 106 provides galvanic isolation between the edge controller 100 and the signalling electronics of each connector station, so that a fault in the power path of one connector station is not communicated to the edge controller 100 or to the remaining connector stations. The isolated local bus 106 may be implemented as a differential serial bus with isolated transceivers at each node, as a set of point-to-point isolated links, or as an optically isolated bus, and its physical form is not essential to the operation described here.

A network interface 108 connects the edge controller 100 to a remote management system. The network interface 108 may be a wired network port, a cellular modem, or a wireless network interface. As described below, the network interface 108 conveys remote schedules and authorizations to the edge controller 100 and conveys uploaded meter records from the edge controller 100, but the safety behaviour of the system does not depend on the availability of the network interface 108.

The connector station

FIG. 2 shows the first connector station 110 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The first connector station 110 comprises a first contactor 120, a first connector current sensor 122, a first control-pilot interface 124, and a first vehicle connector 126. The first contactor 120 is connected in the power path between the branch conductor 102 and the first vehicle connector 126 and, when closed, permits current to flow from the branch conductor 102 to a vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The first connector current sensor 122 measures the connector current flowing in that power path, that is, the current actually drawn by the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126.

The first control-pilot interface 124 presents a control-pilot signal to the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The control-pilot signal advertises a maximum current, called here the assigned limit, that the vehicle is permitted to draw, and reports the state of the coupling, including whether a vehicle is connected and whether that vehicle is requesting energy. The first control-pilot interface 124 therefore serves both as the command path by which an assigned limit reaches the vehicle and as a status path by which the presence of a connected vehicle is reported to the edge controller 100.

Each connector station of the plurality further has a local connector identifier. The local connector identifier is a stored value that distinguishes one connector of the plurality from another in the records, authorizations, and assignments held by the edge controller 100. The local connector identifier is a data value and does not appear as an inscription on the connector station in the drawings.

The distinction between the first control-pilot interface 124 and the first connector current sensor 122 is used throughout this description. The first control-pilot interface 124 carries a command. The first connector current sensor 122 carries a measurement. The edge controller 100 does not treat the assigned limit sent through the first control-pilot interface 124 as evidence of the current that the connector is drawing. It obtains that evidence from the first connector current sensor 122.

The edge controller

FIG. 3 shows the edge controller 100 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The edge controller 100 comprises a processing circuit 130 and a nonvolatile memory 132, and is coupled to the isolated local bus 106 and to the network interface 108. The processing circuit 130 may be a microcontroller, a microprocessor with associated volatile memory, a system on a chip, a programmable logic device, or a combination of such devices, and executes the allocation and protection processes described below. The nonvolatile memory 132 retains stored values across loss of supply, and may be flash memory, electrically erasable programmable read-only memory, ferroelectric memory, or another non-volatile storage device.

The edge controller 100 further comprises a local fault indicator 134 and a service input 136. The local fault indicator 134 provides an indication at the equipment itself, independently of the network interface 108, and may be a lamp, an illuminated legend, a display element, or an audible annunciator. The service input 136 is an input by which an installer places the edge controller 100 in a commissioning mode, and may be a physical control on the equipment, a locally connected service terminal, or a maintenance port that requires physical access to the enclosure of the edge controller 100.

For each active connector of the plurality, the edge controller 100 stores a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. The charging authorization records that the session at that connector is permitted to draw energy. The requested current is the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained, and may be obtained from the vehicle by way of the control-pilot interface of that connector, from the rating of the connector, or from a stored session parameter. The minimum sustaining current is the smallest assigned limit at which the session at that connector is expected to remain charging rather than terminating and requiring a new start, and may be a value that is common to the plurality of connectors or a value stored for each connector individually. The energy-deficit value represents the extent to which the session at that connector has been served less than its requested current over the shared-capacity period. In some implementations the energy-deficit value is accumulated over successive allocation intervals from the difference between the requested current of the session and the current assigned to that session. In other implementations the energy-deficit value is accumulated from the difference between the requested current and the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector, which additionally accounts for a vehicle that draws less than it was permitted to draw. In further implementations the energy-deficit value is derived from a stored energy target for the session and the energy delivered to that session so far. Any of these implementations gives a value that increases while a session is held below its request and decreases as the shortfall is made up, and the allocation process described below uses only that property of the value.

Allocation at each allocation interval

FIG. 4 shows the process carried out by the edge controller 100. The edge controller 100 repeats the allocation portion of the process at each allocation interval. The allocation interval is a recurring period, and its length is chosen so that assigned limits are revised more often than the load on the branch is expected to change materially, while remaining long enough for a vehicle to act on a previously assigned limit.

At an available-charging-current determination step 200, the edge controller 100 subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. The measured non-charging branch load is obtained from the branch current sensor 104 and the connector current sensors: the edge controller 100 takes the difference between the measured branch current and the sum of the connector currents measured at the connector stations, so that the portion of the branch current drawn by the non-charging load 114 is determined by measurement rather than by assumption. The configurable safety reserve is a stored margin that is withheld from allocation, and accommodates the measurement tolerance of the sensors, the step size and settling behaviour of vehicles responding to a changed assigned limit, and any increase in the non-charging load 114 that occurs between allocation intervals. Because the non-charging portion of the branch load is measured at each allocation interval and subtracted at the determination step 200, the available charging current follows the varying load of the site, and capacity released by the non-charging load 114 becomes available to the connectors instead of being permanently withheld.

At a minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, the edge controller 100 first assigns the minimum sustaining current to the sessions that can receive it. The edge controller 100 takes the active connectors in turn and assigns the minimum sustaining current of each to that connector for as long as the available charging current has not been exhausted. A session for which the remaining available charging current is less than its minimum sustaining current cannot receive the minimum sustaining current, and is assigned no current at that allocation interval rather than being assigned a value below its minimum sustaining current. Assigning a value below the minimum sustaining current would be worse than assigning nothing, because the session would be likely to terminate while still consuming allocated capacity, and would then require a new start. Where the available charging current is insufficient for every active session to receive its minimum sustaining current, the edge controller 100 selects the sessions to be sustained in order of energy deficit, so that the sessions that have been served least are sustained first.

At a deficit-based distribution step 204, the edge controller 100 distributes the remaining portion of the available charging current, that is, the portion left after the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, according to energy deficit. Sessions with a greater energy-deficit value receive a greater share of the remaining current than sessions with a smaller energy-deficit value. The distribution may be made in proportion to the energy-deficit values of the sessions, or by allocating to the session with the greatest energy-deficit value until its energy-deficit value falls to that of the next session and then allocating to those sessions together, or by another rule that orders the shares by energy deficit. No session is assigned more than its requested current, and any current that remains after every session has reached its requested current is left unassigned and is therefore added to the margin held on the branch. Distributing by energy deficit rather than by instantaneous request corrects, rather than perpetuates, the inequality that arises when one session begins while the branch is heavily loaded and another begins while it is lightly loaded.

At a limit transmission and connector current verification step 206, the edge controller 100 sends each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector, and then verifies the resulting connector current with the connector current sensor of that connector. Verification comprises comparing the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of a connector with the assigned limit sent to that connector. Where the measured connector current exceeds the assigned limit of that connector, the connector is not honouring the command it has been given, and the edge controller 100 records the deviation for that connector and treats the measured connector current, rather than the assigned limit, as the load that the connector places on the branch at the next allocation interval. The allocation is in this way closed loop at each connector: a connector that draws less than it has been permitted does not cause capacity to be withheld from the others, and a connector that draws more than it has been permitted does not cause the branch to be overcommitted at the next interval.

The branch current sensor as an independent safety input

The branch current sensor 104 is an independent safety input. It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the determination step 200: it governs a protection process that acts on the power path and that does not depend on the cooperation of any vehicle. The protection process is described with continued reference to FIG. 4.

At a pilot reduction step 208, the edge controller 100 compares the measured branch current from the branch current sensor 104 with the branch limit. When the measured branch current is above the branch limit, the edge controller 100 sends a reduced pilot command to at least one connector of the plurality, that is, an assigned limit lower than the limit previously assigned to that connector, and starts a verification interval. The reduced pilot command is the first stage of the response, because reducing current through the control pilot lets a vehicle taper its draw and lets the session continue, which is preferable to interrupting the power path.

At an ordered contactor shedding step 210, the edge controller 100 determines whether the measured branch current remains above the branch limit after the reduced pilot command and after the verification interval has elapsed. The verification interval is long enough for a vehicle that honours the reduced pilot command to have acted on it. If the measured branch current has fallen below the branch limit within the verification interval, the reduced pilot command has been effective and the edge controller 100 returns to the allocation interval process. If the measured branch current remains above the branch limit at the end of the verification interval, the pilot signalling has not produced the required reduction, and the edge controller 100 opens the connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch limit.

The shedding order is stored in the nonvolatile memory 132 and defines the sequence in which the contactors of the plurality of connector stations are opened. The shedding order may be configured at installation, may be arranged so that the most recently started session is opened first, or may be arranged so that the session with the smallest energy-deficit value is opened first, so that the session that has already been served most is the one that gives up its power path. Opening the contactors one at a time, with the measured branch current re-evaluated between openings, removes only as much load as the measurement shows to be necessary: as soon as the measured branch current is below the branch limit, no further contactor is opened, and the remaining sessions continue.

The staged sequence of a reduced pilot command, a verification interval, and then ordered interruption of the power path addresses the technical problem set out in the background. A control-pilot command is advisory, and a vehicle that ignores it, responds too slowly, or responds only in coarse steps leaves the branch loaded above its limit. Allocation that works only from commanded values cannot detect that condition at all. By taking the measured branch current from a sensor that is upstream of every connector contactor, and by treating the persistence of an over-limit measurement through a verification interval as the trigger for opening the power path, the edge controller 100 bounds the branch current with an action that is entirely within its own control, while still giving the cooperative case the opportunity to resolve without interrupting any session.

Recovery after shedding

At a reclose permissive step 212, the edge controller 100 governs the reclosing of a contactor that has been opened by the ordered contactor shedding step 210. The edge controller 100 does not reclose such a contactor until three conditions are satisfied together: the connector current sensor of that connector reports zero current, the control-pilot interface of that connector reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.

Each condition addresses a distinct hazard. A report of zero current from the connector current sensor establishes that the power path is in fact open, so that a reclose command is not issued onto a path that is still carrying current. A report of a connected vehicle from the control-pilot interface establishes that there is a session to restore, so that the power path is not energized to a coupling from which the vehicle has been removed. The randomized recovery delay separates in time the reclosing of the contactors that were shed together, and separates the recovery of the equipment from the recovery of other equipment responding to the same site event, so that the loads do not return in unison and reproduce the overload that the shedding sequence has just relieved. The randomized recovery delay is drawn afresh for each contactor from a configured range, so that two contactors of the plurality do not become synchronized across successive events.

On reclosing, the edge controller 100 resumes the allocation interval process, and the reclosed session takes part in the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202 and the deficit-based distribution step 204 in the ordinary way.

Welded-contactor isolation

At a welded-contactor isolation step 214, the edge controller 100 records a welded-contactor condition for a connector when the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector. The leakage threshold is a stored current magnitude above zero, chosen to be above the residual measurement that the connector current sensor reports on an open path and below any current that would represent load, so that sensor noise and standing offsets are not mistaken for a welded contact.

When the welded-contactor condition has been recorded, the edge controller 100 inhibits the other contactors on the same branch and operates the local fault indicator 134. The other contactors are inhibited because a welded contactor consumes branch capacity that neither the allocation process nor the shedding sequence can recover: the shedding sequence believes that opening that contactor has released the current of that connector, and any further allocation made on that belief would overcommit the branch. Inhibiting the other contactors removes the controllable load from the branch and leaves only the current of the welded connector, which is the safe state available to the edge controller 100 with the means at its disposal. The local fault indicator 134 is operated at the equipment because the condition requires physical service and because it must be annunciated whether or not the network interface 108 is available.

Operation during a network outage

The edge controller 100 can receive remote schedules and authorizations through the network interface 108. A remote schedule may set the branch limit for a period of the day, and a remote authorization may permit a session at a given connector.

The edge controller 100 stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in the nonvolatile memory 132. The signed local authorization token is issued by the remote management system, carries a cryptographic signature that the edge controller 100 verifies against a stored key, identifies the connectors it authorizes by their local connector identifiers, and carries an expiry. The last accepted branch limit is the most recent branch limit that the edge controller 100 has accepted from the remote management system.

During a network outage the edge controller 100 continues already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and the independent branch-current safety process described above. Charging therefore continues through the outage, and continues within a limit that a responsible authority has set, rather than within a limit chosen locally because no other limit is available. The edge controller 100 does not start a newly connected session unless the signed local authorization token authorizes that connector and has not expired. A newly connected vehicle at a connector that the token does not authorize, or a newly connected vehicle at any connector after the token has expired, is not started until communication returns and a fresh authorization is obtained.

Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence held in the nonvolatile memory 132. Each record is appended to the sequence together with a value computed over that record and over the preceding entry of the sequence, so that removal, reordering, or alteration of an entry is detectable from the sequence itself. The records accumulated during the outage are uploaded when communication returns, and the sequence values are uploaded with them, so that the remote management system can confirm that the uploaded run is complete and unaltered.

Installation mapping through the service input

A multi-connector installation is wired by hand, and the identifier a connector is given in configuration must correspond to the physical contactor and the physical current sensor channel that serve that connector. A transposition assigns a current limit intended for one connector to another. Every component continues to function, every sensor continues to report, and the allocation nevertheless governs the wrong power path.

The service input 136 permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors. With the edge controller 100 in the commissioning mode entered through the service input 136, the edge controller 100 commands one low-energy pilot transition at a time, that is, it drives a pilot transition at a single connector, and confirms the corresponding connector current sensor by observing which sensed channel responds to that transition. The transition is a low-energy one, sufficient to produce a distinguishable response at the connector current sensor of the connector that is actually being driven, and the transitions are commanded one at a time so that the responding channel is unambiguous.

The association between a connector identifier and a physical contactor is stored in the nonvolatile memory 132 only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector. If the responding channel is not the channel expected for the commanded connector, or if no channel responds, no association is stored for that connector and the edge controller 100 operates the local fault indicator 134. The mapping is thus established by measurement on the same sensors that the allocation process later relies upon, so a wiring-map error is found at commissioning instead of silently misdirecting current limits for the life of the installation.

General considerations

The allocation process, the branch protection process, the offline authorization behaviour, the welded-contactor isolation, and the installation mapping are described together because they share the sensors and the isolated local bus 106 of a single edge controller 100. They are nevertheless separable. An embodiment may carry out the allocation and branch protection processes without the offline authorization behaviour, without the tamper-evident record sequence, or without the commissioning mode, and an embodiment may include any combination of those additional features.

The processes described above may be embodied as instructions stored on a non-transitory computer-readable medium and executed by the processing circuit 130. The values described as stored, including the branch limit, the configurable safety reserve, the minimum sustaining current, the shedding order, the leakage threshold, the range of the randomized recovery delay, the length of the allocation interval, and the length of the verification interval, may be configured at installation, may be set through the network interface 108, or may be held as defaults in the nonvolatile memory 132.

The terms first and second are used to distinguish one connector station of the plurality from another and do not imply an order of importance or of operation. The system is not limited to two connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each connector station of the plurality. The embodiments described here are illustrative, and a person skilled in the art will recognize that elements described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with elements described in connection with another. The scope of the invention is defined by the claims that follow.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part of this disclosure and show particular embodiments by way of illustration. Other embodiments may be used and structural or logical changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views.

Overview of the system

FIG. 1 shows a charging control system in which an edge controller 100 manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch. A branch conductor 102 supplies the plurality of connectors from a single point of protection. The allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, referred to in this description as the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors that the branch conductor 102 supplies. The branch limit is a stored value that corresponds to the aggregate current the branch is permitted to carry, and may be derived from the rating of the protective device of the branch, from a site limit imposed by the supplying utility or by an energy management authority, or from both.

The branch conductor 102 supplies a first connector station 110 and a second connector station 112. Two connector stations are shown for clarity of illustration. The system accommodates a larger plurality of connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each further connector station of the plurality. The branch conductor 102 also supplies a non-charging load 114, which represents lighting, building services, and other equipment that is connected to the same branch and that is not under the control of the edge controller 100.

A branch current sensor 104 measures total current on the branch conductor 102 upstream of the contactors of the connector stations. Because the branch current sensor 104 is located upstream of those contactors, the current it measures includes both the current drawn by the connector stations and the current drawn by the non-charging load 114. The branch current sensor 104 may be a current transformer, a Rogowski coil, a Hall-effect sensor, a shunt with an isolated amplifier, or another transducer that reports the magnitude of alternating current on a conductor. Where the branch is polyphase, the branch current sensor 104 comprises a transducer for each phase conductor of the branch, and measured branch current is taken as the greatest of the per-phase magnitudes, so that the branch limit governs the most heavily loaded phase.

The edge controller 100 communicates with the connector stations over an isolated local bus 106. The isolated local bus 106 carries assigned current limits and contactor commands from the edge controller 100 to the connector stations, and carries connector current measurements and control-pilot status from the connector stations to the edge controller 100. The isolated local bus 106 provides galvanic isolation between the edge controller 100 and the signalling electronics of each connector station, so that a fault in the power path of one connector station is not communicated to the edge controller 100 or to the remaining connector stations. The isolated local bus 106 may be implemented as a differential serial bus with isolated transceivers at each node, as a set of point-to-point isolated links, or as an optically isolated bus, and its physical form is not essential to the operation described here.

A network interface 108 connects the edge controller 100 to a remote management system. The network interface 108 may be a wired network port, a cellular modem, or a wireless network interface. As described below, the network interface 108 conveys remote schedules and authorizations to the edge controller 100 and conveys uploaded meter records from the edge controller 100, but the safety behaviour of the system does not depend on the availability of the network interface 108.

The connector station

FIG. 2 shows the first connector station 110 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The first connector station 110 comprises a first contactor 120, a first connector current sensor 122, a first control-pilot interface 124, and a first vehicle connector 126. The first contactor 120 is connected in the power path between the branch conductor 102 and the first vehicle connector 126 and, when closed, permits current to flow from the branch conductor 102 to a vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The first connector current sensor 122 measures the connector current flowing in that power path, that is, the current actually drawn by the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126.

The first control-pilot interface 124 presents a control-pilot signal to the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The control-pilot signal advertises a maximum current, called here the assigned limit, that the vehicle is permitted to draw, and reports the state of the coupling, including whether a vehicle is connected and whether that vehicle is requesting energy. The first control-pilot interface 124 therefore serves both as the command path by which an assigned limit reaches the vehicle and as a status path by which the presence of a connected vehicle is reported to the edge controller 100.

Each connector station of the plurality further has a local connector identifier. The local connector identifier is a stored value that distinguishes one connector of the plurality from another in the records, authorizations, and assignments held by the edge controller 100. The local connector identifier is a data value and does not appear as an inscription on the connector station in the drawings.

The distinction between the first control-pilot interface 124 and the first connector current sensor 122 is used throughout this description. The first control-pilot interface 124 carries a command. The first connector current sensor 122 carries a measurement. The edge controller 100 does not treat the assigned limit sent through the first control-pilot interface 124 as evidence of the current that the connector is drawing. It obtains that evidence from the first connector current sensor 122.

The edge controller

FIG. 3 shows the edge controller 100 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The edge controller 100 comprises a processing circuit 130 and a nonvolatile memory 132, and is coupled to the isolated local bus 106 and to the network interface 108. The processing circuit 130 may be a microcontroller, a microprocessor with associated volatile memory, a system on a chip, a programmable logic device, or a combination of such devices, and executes the allocation and protection processes described below. The nonvolatile memory 132 retains stored values across loss of supply, and may be flash memory, electrically erasable programmable read-only memory, ferroelectric memory, or another non-volatile storage device.

The edge controller 100 further comprises a local fault indicator 134 and a service input 136. The local fault indicator 134 provides an indication at the equipment itself, independently of the network interface 108, and may be a lamp, an illuminated legend, a display element, or an audible annunciator. The service input 136 is an input by which an installer places the edge controller 100 in a commissioning mode, and may be a physical control on the equipment, a locally connected service terminal, or a maintenance port that requires physical access to the enclosure of the edge controller 100.

For each active connector of the plurality, the edge controller 100 stores a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. The charging authorization records that the session at that connector is permitted to draw energy. The requested current is the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained, and may be obtained from the vehicle by way of the control-pilot interface of that connector, from the rating of the connector, or from a stored session parameter. The minimum sustaining current is the smallest assigned limit at which the session at that connector is expected to remain charging rather than terminating and requiring a new start, and may be a value that is common to the plurality of connectors or a value stored for each connector individually. The energy-deficit value represents the extent to which the session at that connector has been served less than its requested current over the shared-capacity period. In some implementations the energy-deficit value is accumulated over successive allocation intervals from the difference between the requested current of the session and the current assigned to that session. In other implementations the energy-deficit value is accumulated from the difference between the requested current and the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector, which additionally accounts for a vehicle that draws less than it was permitted to draw. In further implementations the energy-deficit value is derived from a stored energy target for the session and the energy delivered to that session so far. Any of these implementations gives a value that increases while a session is held below its request and decreases as the shortfall is made up, and the allocation process described below uses only that property of the value.

Allocation at each allocation interval

FIG. 4 shows the process carried out by the edge controller 100. The edge controller 100 repeats the allocation portion of the process at each allocation interval. The allocation interval is a recurring period, and its length is chosen so that assigned limits are revised more often than the load on the branch is expected to change materially, while remaining long enough for a vehicle to act on a previously assigned limit.

At an available-charging-current determination step 200, the edge controller 100 subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. The measured non-charging branch load is obtained from the branch current sensor 104 and the connector current sensors: the edge controller 100 takes the difference between the measured branch current and the sum of the connector currents measured at the connector stations, so that the portion of the branch current drawn by the non-charging load 114 is determined by measurement rather than by assumption. The configurable safety reserve is a stored margin that is withheld from allocation, and accommodates the measurement tolerance of the sensors, the step size and settling behaviour of vehicles responding to a changed assigned limit, and any increase in the non-charging load 114 that occurs between allocation intervals. Because the non-charging portion of the branch load is measured at each allocation interval and subtracted at the determination step 200, the available charging current follows the varying load of the site, and capacity released by the non-charging load 114 becomes available to the connectors instead of being permanently withheld.

At a minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, the edge controller 100 first assigns the minimum sustaining current to the sessions that can receive it. The edge controller 100 takes the active connectors in turn and assigns the minimum sustaining current of each to that connector for as long as the available charging current has not been exhausted. A session for which the remaining available charging current is less than its minimum sustaining current cannot receive the minimum sustaining current, and is assigned no current at that allocation interval rather than being assigned a value below its minimum sustaining current. Assigning a value below the minimum sustaining current would be worse than assigning nothing, because the session would be likely to terminate while still consuming allocated capacity, and would then require a new start. Where the available charging current is insufficient for every active session to receive its minimum sustaining current, the edge controller 100 selects the sessions to be sustained in order of energy deficit, so that the sessions that have been served least are sustained first.

At a deficit-based distribution step 204, the edge controller 100 distributes the remaining portion of the available charging current, that is, the portion left after the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, according to energy deficit. Sessions with a greater energy-deficit value receive a greater share of the remaining current than sessions with a smaller energy-deficit value. The distribution may be made in proportion to the energy-deficit values of the sessions, or by allocating to the session with the greatest energy-deficit value until its energy-deficit value falls to that of the next session and then allocating to those sessions together, or by another rule that orders the shares by energy deficit. No session is assigned more than its requested current, and any current that remains after every session has reached its requested current is left unassigned and is therefore added to the margin held on the branch. Distributing by energy deficit rather than by instantaneous request corrects, rather than perpetuates, the inequality that arises when one session begins while the branch is heavily loaded and another begins while it is lightly loaded.

At a limit transmission and connector current verification step 206, the edge controller 100 sends each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector, and then verifies the resulting connector current with the connector current sensor of that connector. Verification comprises comparing the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of a connector with the assigned limit sent to that connector. Where the measured connector current exceeds the assigned limit of that connector, the connector is not honouring the command it has been given, and the edge controller 100 records the deviation for that connector and treats the measured connector current, rather than the assigned limit, as the load that the connector places on the branch at the next allocation interval. The allocation is in this way closed loop at each connector: a connector that draws less than it has been permitted does not cause capacity to be withheld from the others, and a connector that draws more than it has been permitted does not cause the branch to be overcommitted at the next interval.

The branch current sensor as an independent safety input

The branch current sensor 104 is an independent safety input. It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the determination step 200: it governs a protection process that acts on the power path and that does not depend on the cooperation of any vehicle. The protection process is described with continued reference to FIG. 4.

At a pilot reduction step 208, the edge controller 100 compares the measured branch current from the branch current sensor 104 with the branch limit. When the measured branch current is above the branch limit, the edge controller 100 sends a reduced pilot command to at least one connector of the plurality, that is, an assigned limit lower than the limit previously assigned to that connector, and starts a verification interval. The reduced pilot command is the first stage of the response, because reducing current through the control pilot lets a vehicle taper its draw and lets the session continue, which is preferable to interrupting the power path.

At an ordered contactor shedding step 210, the edge controller 100 determines whether the measured branch current remains above the branch limit after the reduced pilot command and after the verification interval has elapsed. The verification interval is long enough for a vehicle that honours the reduced pilot command to have acted on it. If the measured branch current has fallen below the branch limit within the verification interval, the reduced pilot command has been effective and the edge controller 100 returns to the allocation interval process. If the measured branch current remains above the branch limit at the end of the verification interval, the pilot signalling has not produced the required reduction, and the edge controller 100 opens the connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch limit.

The shedding order is stored in the nonvolatile memory 132 and defines the sequence in which the contactors of the plurality of connector stations are opened. The shedding order may be configured at installation, may be arranged so that the most recently started session is opened first, or may be arranged so that the session with the smallest energy-deficit value is opened first, so that the session that has already been served most is the one that gives up its power path. Opening the contactors one at a time, with the measured branch current re-evaluated between openings, removes only as much load as the measurement shows to be necessary: as soon as the measured branch current is below the branch limit, no further contactor is opened, and the remaining sessions continue.

The staged sequence of a reduced pilot command, a verification interval, and then ordered interruption of the power path addresses the technical problem set out in the background. A control-pilot command is advisory, and a vehicle that ignores it, responds too slowly, or responds only in coarse steps leaves the branch loaded above its limit. Allocation that works only from commanded values cannot detect that condition at all. By taking the measured branch current from a sensor that is upstream of every connector contactor, and by treating the persistence of an over-limit measurement through a verification interval as the trigger for opening the power path, the edge controller 100 bounds the branch current with an action that is entirely within its own control, while still giving the cooperative case the opportunity to resolve without interrupting any session.

Recovery after shedding

At a reclose permissive step 212, the edge controller 100 governs the reclosing of a contactor that has been opened by the ordered contactor shedding step 210. The edge controller 100 does not reclose such a contactor until three conditions are satisfied together: the connector current sensor of that connector reports zero current, the control-pilot interface of that connector reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.

Each condition addresses a distinct hazard. A report of zero current from the connector current sensor establishes that the power path is in fact open, so that a reclose command is not issued onto a path that is still carrying current. A report of a connected vehicle from the control-pilot interface establishes that there is a session to restore, so that the power path is not energized to a coupling from which the vehicle has been removed. The randomized recovery delay separates in time the reclosing of the contactors that were shed together, and separates the recovery of the equipment from the recovery of other equipment responding to the same site event, so that the loads do not return in unison and reproduce the overload that the shedding sequence has just relieved. The randomized recovery delay is drawn afresh for each contactor from a configured range, so that two contactors of the plurality do not become synchronized across successive events.

On reclosing, the edge controller 100 resumes the allocation interval process, and the reclosed session takes part in the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202 and the deficit-based distribution step 204 in the ordinary way.

Welded-contactor isolation

At a welded-contactor isolation step 214, the edge controller 100 records a welded-contactor condition for a connector when the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector. The leakage threshold is a stored current magnitude above zero, chosen to be above the residual measurement that the connector current sensor reports on an open path and below any current that would represent load, so that sensor noise and standing offsets are not mistaken for a welded contact.

When the welded-contactor condition has been recorded, the edge controller 100 inhibits the other contactors on the same branch and operates the local fault indicator 134. The other contactors are inhibited because a welded contactor consumes branch capacity that neither the allocation process nor the shedding sequence can recover: the shedding sequence believes that opening that contactor has released the current of that connector, and any further allocation made on that belief would overcommit the branch. Inhibiting the other contactors removes the controllable load from the branch and leaves only the current of the welded connector, which is the safe state available to the edge controller 100 with the means at its disposal. The local fault indicator 134 is operated at the equipment because the condition requires physical service and because it must be annunciated whether or not the network interface 108 is available.

Operation during a network outage

The edge controller 100 can receive remote schedules and authorizations through the network interface 108. A remote schedule may set the branch limit for a period of the day, and a remote authorization may permit a session at a given connector.

The edge controller 100 stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in the nonvolatile memory 132. The signed local authorization token is issued by the remote management system, carries a cryptographic signature that the edge controller 100 verifies against a stored key, identifies the connectors it authorizes by their local connector identifiers, and carries an expiry. The last accepted branch limit is the most recent branch limit that the edge controller 100 has accepted from the remote management system.

During a network outage the edge controller 100 continues already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and the independent branch-current safety process described above. Charging therefore continues through the outage, and continues within a limit that a responsible authority has set, rather than within a limit chosen locally because no other limit is available. The edge controller 100 does not start a newly connected session unless the signed local authorization token authorizes that connector and has not expired. A newly connected vehicle at a connector that the token does not authorize, or a newly connected vehicle at any connector after the token has expired, is not started until communication returns and a fresh authorization is obtained.

Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence held in the nonvolatile memory 132. Each record is appended to the sequence together with a value computed over that record and over the preceding entry of the sequence, so that removal, reordering, or alteration of an entry is detectable from the sequence itself. The records accumulated during the outage are uploaded when communication returns, and the sequence values are uploaded with them, so that the remote management system can confirm that the uploaded run is complete and unaltered.

Installation mapping through the service input

A multi-connector installation is wired by hand, and the identifier a connector is given in configuration must correspond to the physical contactor and the physical current sensor channel that serve that connector. A transposition assigns a current limit intended for one connector to another. Every component continues to function, every sensor continues to report, and the allocation nevertheless governs the wrong power path.

The service input 136 permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors. With the edge controller 100 in the commissioning mode entered through the service input 136, the edge controller 100 commands one low-energy pilot transition at a time, that is, it drives a pilot transition at a single connector, and confirms the corresponding connector current sensor by observing which sensed channel responds to that transition. The transition is a low-energy one, sufficient to produce a distinguishable response at the connector current sensor of the connector that is actually being driven, and the transitions are commanded one at a time so that the responding channel is unambiguous.

The association between a connector identifier and a physical contactor is stored in the nonvolatile memory 132 only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector. If the responding channel is not the channel expected for the commanded connector, or if no channel responds, no association is stored for that connector. The mapping is thus established by measurement on the same sensors that the allocation process later relies upon, so a wiring-map error is found at commissioning instead of silently misdirecting current limits for the life of the installation.

General considerations

The allocation process, the branch protection process, the offline authorization behaviour, the welded-contactor isolation, and the installation mapping are described together because they share the sensors and the isolated local bus 106 of a single edge controller 100. They are nevertheless separable. An embodiment may carry out the allocation and branch protection processes without the offline authorization behaviour, without the tamper-evident record sequence, or without the commissioning mode, and an embodiment may include any combination of those additional features.

The processes described above may be embodied as instructions stored on a non-transitory computer-readable medium and executed by the processing circuit 130. The values described as stored, including the branch limit, the configurable safety reserve, the minimum sustaining current, the shedding order, the leakage threshold, the range of the randomized recovery delay, the length of the allocation interval, and the length of the verification interval, may be configured at installation, may be set through the network interface 108, or may be held as defaults in the nonvolatile memory 132.

The terms first and second are used to distinguish one connector station of the plurality from another and do not imply an order of importance or of operation. The system is not limited to two connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each connector station of the plurality. The embodiments described here are illustrative, and a person skilled in the art will recognize that elements described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with elements described in connection with another. The scope of the invention is defined by the claims that follow.

lines: At an available-charging-current determination step 200, the edge controller 100 subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. The measured non-charging branch load is obtained from the branch current sensor 104 and the connector current sensors: the edge controller 100 takes the difference between the measured branch current and the sum of the connector currents measured at the connector stations, so that the portion of the branch current drawn by the non-charging load 114 is determined by measurement rather than by assumption. The configurable safety reserve is a stored margin that is withheld from allocation, and accommodates the measurement tolerance of the sensors, the step size and settling behaviour of vehicles responding to a changed assigned limit, and any increase in the non-charging load 114 that occurs between allocation intervals. Because the non-charging portion of the branch load is measured at each allocation interval and subtracted at the determination step 200, the available charging current follows the varying load of the site, and capacity released by the non-charging load 114 becomes available to the connectors instead of being permanently withheld.

-At a minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, the edge controller 100 first assigns the minimum sustaining current to the sessions that can receive it. The edge controller 100 takes the active connectors in turn and assigns the minimum sustaining current of each to that connector for as long as the available charging current has not been exhausted. A session for which the remaining available charging current is less than its minimum sustaining current cannot receive the minimum sustaining current, and is assigned no current at that allocation interval rather than being assigned a value below its minimum sustaining current. Assigning a value below the minimum sustaining current would be worse than assigning nothing, because the session would be likely to terminate while still consuming allocated capacity, and would then require a new start. Where the available charging current is insufficient for every active session to receive its minimum sustaining current, the edge controller 100 selects the sessions to be sustained in order of energy deficit, so that the sessions that have been served least are sustained first.

+At a minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, the edge controller 100 first assigns the minimum sustaining current to the sessions that can receive it. The edge controller 100 takes the active connectors in turn and assigns the minimum sustaining current of each to that connector for as long as the available charging current has not been exhausted. A session for which a remaining part of the available charging current at that allocation interval is less than its minimum sustaining current cannot receive the minimum sustaining current, and is assigned no current at that allocation interval rather than being assigned a value below its minimum sustaining current. Assigning a value below the minimum sustaining current would be worse than assigning nothing, because the session would be likely to terminate while still consuming allocated capacity, and would then require a new start. Where the available charging current is insufficient for every active session to receive its minimum sustaining current, the edge controller 100 selects the sessions to be sustained in order of energy deficit, so that the sessions that have been served least are sustained first.

At a deficit-based distribution step 204, the edge controller 100 distributes the remaining portion of the available charging current, that is, the portion left after the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, according to energy deficit. Sessions with a greater energy-deficit value receive a greater share of the remaining current than sessions with a smaller energy-deficit value. The distribution may be made in proportion to the energy-deficit values of the sessions, or by allocating to the session with the greatest energy-deficit value until its energy-deficit value falls to that of the next session and then allocating to those sessions together, or by another rule that orders the shares by energy deficit. No session is assigned more than its requested current, and any current that remains after every session has reached its requested current is left unassigned and is therefore added to the margin held on the branch. Distributing by energy deficit rather than by instantaneous request corrects, rather than perpetuates, the inequality that arises when one session begins while the branch is heavily loaded and another begins while it is lightly loaded.

input.summary: Wrote the complete first draft of the application from the inventor's disclosure: all ten body files in draft/, the reference-numeral table, and four figure specifications (system block diagram, connector-station detail, edge-controller detail, and a process flow of the allocation interval plus the staged branch-protection sequence). Claim set is 20 claims in three statutory classes: system (1 to 14), method (15 to 19), and non-transitory computer-readable medium (20). Important caveat on prior art: prior_art/ contains only INDEX.md and that index lists no references, so the art you gave me may be incomplete and this draft contains no citations. The Background states the technical problems the invention solves in neutral terms, without attributing any teaching to a document I was not given. If a search is run later, the Background is written so that specific references can be cited into it without restructuring the argument.
reasoning: Claim 1 recites the relationship the disclosure itself calls essential, and nothing more: dual sensing (per-connector current sensors plus a branch current sensor upstream of every connector contactor), allocation from an available charging current obtained by subtracting a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve, minimum sustaining current first then energy-deficit distribution, pilot transmission with verification at the connector current sensor, and the staged response of a reduced pilot command followed, if the measured branch current does not respond within a verification interval, by opening contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order. The one-at-a-time ordered shedding gated on a persisting upstream measurement is the limitation doing the real technical work: it bounds branch current by an action wholly inside the controller's power path rather than by a command the vehicle may ignore, and it removes only as much load as the measurement shows to be necessary.

Deliberately kept out of claim 1: the reclose permissives, the welded-contactor detection, the offline token, the tamper-evident record sequence, the commissioning mapping, and the arithmetic for deriving the non-charging load. Each is a separate protective or operational feature that a competitor could omit while still practising the core loop, so each became a dependent claim rather than scope given away for free.

The dependent ladder is graduated rather than decorative. Claim 2 is the next-narrowest fallback, adding the concrete derivation of the non-charging branch load as branch current minus the sum of connector currents. Claims 3 and 4 add the three-condition reclose permissive and the independently drawn randomized delay. Claims 5 and 6 add welded-contactor detection against a leakage threshold and the isolation response. Claims 7 to 9 cover offline operation and the hash-chained meter sequence. Claim 10 covers the commissioning mapping. Claims 11 to 13 cover the sustaining-current behaviour and the closed-loop verification response. Claim 14 covers the polyphase case. Each is a feature that can be argued on its own.
Statutory classes: system, method, and non-transitory medium, because the equipment maker, the site operator running the process, and a firmware supplier are different parties.

The description was widened past the bare disclosure only where a claim term needed enabling support, and always as disclosed alternatives rather than invented facts: the energy-deficit value is described functionally with three example ways to accumulate it, all sharing the property the allocation actually uses; the shedding order, safety reserve, leakage threshold, and interval lengths are described as stored configurable values without inventing numbers; the polyphase branch sensor and the isolated bus implementations are given as alternatives.

One behaviour that crept into an early pass of the commissioning section, operating the local fault indicator when the sensed channel disagrees with the commanded connector, was removed. The disclosure says only that the association is not stored unless the channels agree, and I did not want an unsupported behaviour in the specification.

Figures were split to respect the eight-numeral-per-sheet cap without crowding: FIG. 1 carries the system-level numerals (8), FIG. 2 the connector-station detail (6), FIG. 3 the controller detail (7), and FIG. 4 the eight process steps. No section views were used, so no cutting-plane annotation was needed.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/ contains only INDEX.md, and that index lists no references, so there was nothing to read, nothing to cite, and no document whose combination I could inspect. The draft therefore contains no citations anywhere, which is the correct handling of an empty index: every listed reference must be addressed, and none are listed. Because I could not clear the claims against actual documents, I built the claim set so that the distinguishing work is done by features the disclosure itself identifies as the invention rather than by generic recitations. Claim 1 turns on the measured upstream branch current governing a power-path action, ordered one-at-a-time contactor opening in a stored order, triggered only by persistence of the over-limit measurement through a verification interval after a reduced pilot command, combined with per-connector closed-loop verification and deficit-ordered allocation of a measured available charging current. Terminology was chosen to be accurate for this invention rather than borrowed from generic load-management vocabulary: branch limit, available charging current, minimum sustaining current, energy-deficit value, stored shedding order, verification interval, randomized recovery delay. The Background sets out, before it is needed, the technical reason each of these exists, in particular that a control-pilot value is a command and not a measurement, so that a later argument over any reference that allocates from commanded values has a written foundation. The dependent ladder gives distinct retreat positions (measured non-charging load derivation, three-condition reclose permissive, leakage-threshold welded-contactor isolation, signed offline token, hash-chained meter records, sensor-confirmed commissioning mapping) in case a search later turns up art against the broadest claim. If you run a search, the strongest candidates to check are dynamic load management for multi-outlet EVSE, contactor welding detection in charging equipment, and OCPP-style offline authorization caching.

One behaviour that crept into an early pass of the commissioning section, operating the local fault indicator when the sensed channel disagrees with the commanded connector, was removed. The disclosure says only that the association is not stored unless the channels agree, and I did not want an unsupported behaviour in the specification.

Figures were split to respect the eight-numeral-per-sheet cap without crowding: FIG. 1 carries the system-level numerals (8), FIG. 2 the connector-station detail (6), FIG. 3 the controller detail (7), and FIG. 4 the eight process steps. No section views were used, so no cutting-plane annotation was needed.
