structured_output.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/ contains only INDEX.md, and that index lists no references, so there was nothing to read, nothing to cite, and no document whose combination I could inspect. The draft therefore contains no citations anywhere, which is the correct handling of an empty index: every listed reference must be addressed, and none are listed. Because I could not clear the claims against actual documents, I built the claim set so that the distinguishing work is done by features the disclosure itself identifies as the invention rather than by generic recitations. Claim 1 turns on the measured upstream branch current governing a power-path action, ordered one-at-a-time contactor opening in a stored order, triggered only by persistence of the over-limit measurement through a verification interval after a reduced pilot command, combined with per-connector closed-loop verification and deficit-ordered allocation of a measured available charging current. Terminology was chosen to be accurate for this invention rather than borrowed from generic load-management vocabulary: branch limit, available charging current, minimum sustaining current, energy-deficit value, stored shedding order, verification interval, randomized recovery delay. The Background sets out, before it is needed, the technical reason each of these exists, in particular that a control-pilot value is a command and not a measurement, so that a later argument over any reference that allocates from commanded values has a written foundation. The dependent ladder gives distinct retreat positions (measured non-charging load derivation, three-condition reclose permissive, leakage-threshold welded-contactor isolation, signed offline token, hash-chained meter records, sensor-confirmed commissioning mapping) in case a search later turns up art against the broadest claim. If you run a search, the strongest candidates to check are dynamic load management for multi-outlet EVSE, contactor welding detection in charging equipment, and OCPP-style offline authorization caching.

The complete draft is written. draft/ holds all ten body sections, draft/numerals.md holds 24 numerals each bound to a single part name, and figures/ holds four self-contained drawing specifications (fig-01 system block diagram, fig-02 connector-station detail, fig-03 edge-controller detail, fig-04 process flow), each within the 2800-character limit and the eight-numeral-per-sheet cap.

Claim 1 is a system claim reciting the relationship the disclosure identifies as essential: per-connector current sensing and control-pilot signalling, an upstream branch current sensor, allocation of an available charging current obtained by subtracting a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit, minimum sustaining current assigned first and the remainder distributed by energy deficit, each assigned limit sent on the pilot and verified at the connector current sensor, and, when the measured branch current stays above the branch limit after a reduced pilot command and a verification interval, opening contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order. Claim 15 is the corresponding method and claim 20 a non-transitory medium. Thirteen system dependents and four method dependents give a graduated fallback ladder: measured non-charging load derivation, three-condition reclose permissive, per-contactor randomized delay, leakage-threshold welded-contactor detection and isolation with a local fault indicator, signed offline token and last accepted branch limit, refusal to start unauthorized new sessions offline, hash-chained meter records, sensor-confirmed commissioning mapping, sustaining-current and verification behaviours, and the polyphase case.

One thing to know before filing: prior_art/ contains only an index that lists no references. I had no art to write around and the draft contains no citations, so the art behind this draft may be incomplete. The Background is written so that references found by a later search can be cited into it without restructuring the argument, and it already sets out, in the specification where a later argument needs it, why a control-pilot value is a command rather than a measurement and why the staged pilot-then-shed sequence follows from that.

1	An edge controller manages charging at electric-vehicle connectors supplied by one branch whose branch limit is lower than the sum of the connector ratings. Each connector has a contactor, a connector current sensor, and a control-pilot interface, and a branch current sensor measures current upstream of the contactors. At each allocation interval the controller subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current, assigns a minimum sustaining current to the sessions that can receive it, distributes the remainder according to energy deficit, sends each assigned limit through the corresponding control-pilot interface, and verifies the resulting connector current. When measured branch current remains above the branch limit after a reduced pilot command and a verification interval, the controller opens contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until measured branch current is below the branch limit.

# Previous review - verdict: fail

Reviewed disclosure.md, conversation.md (single USER passage, identical to the disclosure), brief.md, all ten draft sections, numerals.md, and the four figure briefs. The prior art given may be incomplete; no prior-art references are cited in the Background, so no citation tracing was required here. No section lines or sectional views exist in any figure brief, so the v9 section-line designation check is vacuous - nothing to report there. No drafting notes, placeholders, open questions, or unresolved alternatives remain in the draft files.

The core spine traces cleanly: the branch limit below the sum of connector ratings, per-connector contactor / connector current sensor / control-pilot interface / local connector identifier, the upstream branch current sensor, the isolated local bus to the connector interfaces and contactors, the four stored per-session values, the subtract-non-charging-load-and-safety-reserve allocation, minimum-sustaining-then-deficit distribution, pilot transmission with connector-current verification, the reduced-pilot-command / verification-interval / ordered-shedding staging, the three-condition reclose permissive, welded-contactor recording with inhibition of the other contactors and a local fault indicator, offline token and last-accepted-branch-limit behaviour, tamper-evident meter records, and service-input commissioning mapping.

Twenty findings fall outside that spine. The most serious is a three-way conflict about how the branch current sensor reaches the controller: claims 1 and 20 recite the controller "coupled ... to the branch current sensor over the isolated local bus," the FIG. 1 brief draws a dedicated separate line from sensor 104 to the top edge of controller 100 with "No block ... drawn on this line," the FIG. 3 brief shows no branch-sensor port at all, and the disclosure places only "the connector interfaces and contactors" on that bus. That is simultaneously an unsupported claim limitation and an internal inconsistency.

A second group is unsupported technical mechanism recited in dependent claims: the non-charging load derived as branch current minus the sum of connector currents (claims 2, 16 and step 200); per-contactor randomized delays drawn from a configured range (claim 4); polyphase per-phase transducers with a greatest-magnitude rule (claim 14); the compare-and-substitute verification rule (claim 13); assigning zero rather than a sub-minimum current (claim 11); deficit-ordered selection of which sessions are sustained (claim 12); and the chained value computed over each meter record and the preceding entry (claim 9). The disclosure states each corresponding concept only at the level of "measured non-charging branch load," "a randomized recovery delay," "verifies the resulting connector current," "sessions that can receive it," and "a tamper-evident local sequence." None of the mechanisms above appears in any USER passage.

A third group is optional-embodiment prose in the detailed description that the inventor never supplied: three alternative constructions of the energy-deficit value; three alternative shedding-order rules; two alternative deficit-distribution algorithms; the requested-current sources; the per-connector-or-common minimum sustaining current; branch-limit derivation from a protective-device rating or utility/energy-management site limit; the remote schedule setting the branch limit "for a period of the day"; the no-session-above-its-request / surplus-left-unassigned rule; the galvanic-isolation function and three bus implementations; and the hardware menus for the branch current sensor, network interface, processing circuit, nonvolatile memory, local fault indicator, and service input. The identification of non-charging load 114 as "lighting, building services, and other equipment" is drawn from the Background's prior-art framing, not from any inventor passage. The non-transitory computer-readable medium class (claim 20, summary, description) likewise has no disclosure antecedent.

Remaining findings are internal: network interface 108 sits outside edge controller 100 in FIG. 1 but inside its enclosure in FIG. 3 while the text says the controller is "coupled to" it; claim 7 restates the safety process as direct shedding on an over-limit measurement, dropping the staged pilot reduction that claim 1 makes mandatory; the FIG. 2 series order placing sensor 122 downstream of contactor 120 is a topology choice with no source; and description line 21's remark that the identifier "does not appear as an inscription ... in the drawings" is a renderer-justification note that should not remain in the application text. The title also adds subject matter beyond the brief's working title.

Every finding below quotes the candidate wording, quotes or names the nearest source passage showing the gap, and gives a filing-clean fix.

- **[critical] Non-charging load 114 identified as lighting and building services on the strength of Background prose only** (draft/08-detailed-description.md para. at line 7; figures/FIG-1.md geometry bullets 9-10) - The disclosure refers only to "measured non-charging branch load". The identification of that load as lighting, building services, and other equipment appears in the Background as prior-art framing, and prior-art characterization cannot support invention text. The detailed description carries the identification into the described embodiment, and FIG. 1 gives it a numbered block on the branch.
  - Suggested fix: In draft/08-detailed-description.md line 7, replace that sentence with "The branch conductor 102 also supplies a non-charging load 114, which is load connected to the same branch that is not under the control of the edge controller 100." No change to the FIG. 1 geometry is required, since the block itself corresponds to the disclosed non-charging branch load.

Under the disclosed two-stage process such a session could still receive a share at the deficit-distribution stage. The candidate affirmatively forecloses that by assigning zero, which is added allocation substance and also narrows the disclosed process.
  - Suggested fix: Delete claim 11 and renumber the remaining claims (claim 12 is separately deleted above). In draft/08-detailed-description.md line 39, delete ", and is assigned no current at that allocation interval rather than being assigned a value below its minimum sustaining current" and delete the following sentence "Assigning a value below the minimum sustaining current would be worse than assigning nothing, because the session would be likely to terminate while still consuming allocated capacity, and would then require a new start."
- **[major] Non-transitory computer-readable medium embodiment has no disclosure antecedent** (draft/09-claims.md claim 20; draft/06-summary.md para. at line 17; draft/08-detailed-description.md para. at line 93) - The disclosure describes a controller and processes but never mentions software, stored instructions, a processing circuit executing instructions, or a computer-readable medium. Claim 20 recites a distinct article of manufacture built on structure that no USER passage supplies.

This rectangle is the network interface 108, shown schematically. A short line extends from the left side of the network interface 108 and terminates inside the drawing area."

Claim 7, which depends on claim 1, recites shedding conditioned only on the measured branch current remaining above the last accepted branch limit, describing a different, unstaged trigger. That conflicts with claim 1 and with the description, which states that the staged sequence is what governs, and it also departs from the inventor's phrase "the independent branch-current safety process".
  - Suggested fix: In claim 7, replace "and subject to opening the contactors in the stored shedding order when the measured branch current remains above the last accepted branch limit" with "and subject to the reduced pilot command and the opening of the contactors in the stored shedding order recited in claim 1, applied with the last accepted branch limit as the branch limit".

It is a drafting note about the figures rather than a description of the invention, and drawing conventions must stay confined to the figure briefs.

The brief asserts a specific series order, which is a technical relationship rather than a shape convention.

Do not add any corresponding statement to the application text.

The draft title appends two additional characterizations. The added words are technically consistent with the disclosure's stated essential relationship, but the expansion is a formality departure from the brief.

1	In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part of this disclosure and show particular embodiments by way of illustration. Other embodiments may be used and structural or logical changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views.
2	
3	Overview of the system
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a charging control system in which an edge controller 100 manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch. A branch conductor 102 supplies the plurality of connectors from a single point of protection. The allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, referred to in this description as the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors that the branch conductor 102 supplies. The branch limit is a stored value that corresponds to the aggregate current the branch is permitted to carry, and may be derived from the rating of the protective device of the branch, from a site limit imposed by the supplying utility or by an energy management authority, or from both.
6	
7	The branch conductor 102 supplies a first connector station 110 and a second connector station 112. Two connector stations are shown for clarity of illustration. The system accommodates a larger plurality of connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each further connector station of the plurality. The branch conductor 102 also supplies a non-charging load 114, which represents lighting, building services, and other equipment that is connected to the same branch and that is not under the control of the edge controller 100.
8	
9	A branch current sensor 104 measures total current on the branch conductor 102 upstream of the contactors of the connector stations. Because the branch current sensor 104 is located upstream of those contactors, the current it measures includes both the current drawn by the connector stations and the current drawn by the non-charging load 114. The branch current sensor 104 may be a current transformer, a Rogowski coil, a Hall-effect sensor, a shunt with an isolated amplifier, or another transducer that reports the magnitude of alternating current on a conductor. Where the branch is polyphase, the branch current sensor 104 comprises a transducer for each phase conductor of the branch, and measured branch current is taken as the greatest of the per-phase magnitudes, so that the branch limit governs the most heavily loaded phase.
10	
11	The edge controller 100 communicates with the connector stations over an isolated local bus 106. The isolated local bus 106 carries assigned current limits and contactor commands from the edge controller 100 to the connector stations, and carries connector current measurements and control-pilot status from the connector stations to the edge controller 100. The isolated local bus 106 provides galvanic isolation between the edge controller 100 and the signalling electronics of each connector station, so that a fault in the power path of one connector station is not communicated to the edge controller 100 or to the remaining connector stations. The isolated local bus 106 may be implemented as a differential serial bus with isolated transceivers at each node, as a set of point-to-point isolated links, or as an optically isolated bus, and its physical form is not essential to the operation described here.
12	
13	A network interface 108 connects the edge controller 100 to a remote management system. The network interface 108 may be a wired network port, a cellular modem, or a wireless network interface. As described below, the network interface 108 conveys remote schedules and authorizations to the edge controller 100 and conveys uploaded meter records from the edge controller 100, but the safety behaviour of the system does not depend on the availability of the network interface 108.
14	
15	The connector station
16	
17	FIG. 2 shows the first connector station 110 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The first connector station 110 comprises a first contactor 120, a first connector current sensor 122, a first control-pilot interface 124, and a first vehicle connector 126. The first contactor 120 is connected in the power path between the branch conductor 102 and the first vehicle connector 126 and, when closed, permits current to flow from the branch conductor 102 to a vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The first connector current sensor 122 measures the connector current flowing in that power path, that is, the current actually drawn by the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126.
18	
19	The first control-pilot interface 124 presents a control-pilot signal to the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The control-pilot signal advertises a maximum current, called here the assigned limit, that the vehicle is permitted to draw, and reports the state of the coupling, including whether a vehicle is connected and whether that vehicle is requesting energy. The first control-pilot interface 124 therefore serves both as the command path by which an assigned limit reaches the vehicle and as a status path by which the presence of a connected vehicle is reported to the edge controller 100.
20	
21	Each connector station of the plurality further has a local connector identifier. The local connector identifier is a stored value that distinguishes one connector of the plurality from another in the records, authorizations, and assignments held by the edge controller 100. The local connector identifier is a data value and does not appear as an inscription on the connector station in the drawings.
22	
23	The distinction between the first control-pilot interface 124 and the first connector current sensor 122 is used throughout this description. The first control-pilot interface 124 carries a command. The first connector current sensor 122 carries a measurement. The edge controller 100 does not treat the assigned limit sent through the first control-pilot interface 124 as evidence of the current that the connector is drawing. It obtains that evidence from the first connector current sensor 122.
24	
25	The edge controller
26	
27	FIG. 3 shows the edge controller 100 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The edge controller 100 comprises a processing circuit 130 and a nonvolatile memory 132, and is coupled to the isolated local bus 106 and to the network interface 108. The processing circuit 130 may be a microcontroller, a microprocessor with associated volatile memory, a system on a chip, a programmable logic device, or a combination of such devices, and executes the allocation and protection processes described below. The nonvolatile memory 132 retains stored values across loss of supply, and may be flash memory, electrically erasable programmable read-only memory, ferroelectric memory, or another non-volatile storage device.
28	
29	The edge controller 100 further comprises a local fault indicator 134 and a service input 136. The local fault indicator 134 provides an indication at the equipment itself, independently of the network interface 108, and may be a lamp, an illuminated legend, a display element, or an audible annunciator. The service input 136 is an input by which an installer places the edge controller 100 in a commissioning mode, and may be a physical control on the equipment, a locally connected service terminal, or a maintenance port that requires physical access to the enclosure of the edge controller 100.
30	
31	For each active connector of the plurality, the edge controller 100 stores a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. The charging authorization records that the session at that connector is permitted to draw energy. The requested current is the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained, and may be obtained from the vehicle by way of the control-pilot interface of that connector, from the rating of the connector, or from a stored session parameter. The minimum sustaining current is the smallest assigned limit at which the session at that connector is expected to remain charging rather than terminating and requiring a new start, and may be a value that is common to the plurality of connectors or a value stored for each connector individually. The energy-deficit value represents the extent to which the session at that connector has been served less than its requested current over the shared-capacity period. In some implementations the energy-deficit value is accumulated over successive allocation intervals from the difference between the requested current of the session and the current assigned to that session. In other implementations the energy-deficit value is accumulated from the difference between the requested current and the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector, which additionally accounts for a vehicle that draws less than it was permitted to draw. In further implementations the energy-deficit value is derived from a stored energy target for the session and the energy delivered to that session so far. Any of these implementations gives a value that increases while a session is held below its request and decreases as the shortfall is made up, and the allocation process described below uses only that property of the value.
32	
33	Allocation at each allocation interval
34	
35	FIG. 4 shows the process carried out by the edge controller 100. The edge controller 100 repeats the allocation portion of the process at each allocation interval. The allocation interval is a recurring period, and its length is chosen so that assigned limits are revised more often than the load on the branch is expected to change materially, while remaining long enough for a vehicle to act on a previously assigned limit.
36	
37	At an available-charging-current determination step 200, the edge controller 100 subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. The measured non-charging branch load is obtained from the branch current sensor 104 and the connector current sensors: the edge controller 100 takes the difference between the measured branch current and the sum of the connector currents measured at the connector stations, so that the portion of the branch current drawn by the non-charging load 114 is determined by measurement rather than by assumption. The configurable safety reserve is a stored margin that is withheld from allocation, and accommodates the measurement tolerance of the sensors, the step size and settling behaviour of vehicles responding to a changed assigned limit, and any increase in the non-charging load 114 that occurs between allocation intervals. Because the non-charging portion of the branch load is measured at each allocation interval and subtracted at the determination step 200, the available charging current follows the varying load of the site, and capacity released by the non-charging load 114 becomes available to the connectors instead of being permanently withheld.
38	
39	At a minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, the edge controller 100 first assigns the minimum sustaining current to the sessions that can receive it. The edge controller 100 takes the active connectors in turn and assigns the minimum sustaining current of each to that connector for as long as the available charging current has not been exhausted. A session for which a remaining part of the available charging current at that allocation interval is less than its minimum sustaining current cannot receive the minimum sustaining current, and is assigned no current at that allocation interval rather than being assigned a value below its minimum sustaining current. Assigning a value below the minimum sustaining current would be worse than assigning nothing, because the session would be likely to terminate while still consuming allocated capacity, and would then require a new start. Where the available charging current is insufficient for every active session to receive its minimum sustaining current, the edge controller 100 selects the sessions to be sustained in order of energy deficit, so that the sessions that have been served least are sustained first.
40	
41	At a deficit-based distribution step 204, the edge controller 100 distributes the remaining portion of the available charging current, that is, the portion left after the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, according to energy deficit. Sessions with a greater energy-deficit value receive a greater share of the remaining current than sessions with a smaller energy-deficit value. The distribution may be made in proportion to the energy-deficit values of the sessions, or by allocating to the session with the greatest energy-deficit value until its energy-deficit value falls to that of the next session and then allocating to those sessions together, or by another rule that orders the shares by energy deficit. No session is assigned more than its requested current, and any current that remains after every session has reached its requested current is left unassigned and is therefore added to the margin held on the branch. Distributing by energy deficit rather than by instantaneous request corrects, rather than perpetuates, the inequality that arises when one session begins while the branch is heavily loaded and another begins while it is lightly loaded.
42	
43	At a limit transmission and connector current verification step 206, the edge controller 100 sends each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector, and then verifies the resulting connector current with the connector current sensor of that connector. Verification comprises comparing the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of a connector with the assigned limit sent to that connector. Where the measured connector current exceeds the assigned limit of that connector, the connector is not honouring the command it has been given, and the edge controller 100 records the deviation for that connector and treats the measured connector current, rather than the assigned limit, as the load that the connector places on the branch at the next allocation interval. The allocation is in this way closed loop at each connector: a connector that draws less than it has been permitted does not cause capacity to be withheld from the others, and a connector that draws more than it has been permitted does not cause the branch to be overcommitted at the next interval.
44	
45	The branch current sensor as an independent safety input
46	
47	The branch current sensor 104 is an independent safety input. It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the determination step 200: it governs a protection process that acts on the power path and that does not depend on the cooperation of any vehicle. The protection process is described with continued reference to FIG. 4.
48	
49	At a pilot reduction step 208, the edge controller 100 compares the measured branch current from the branch current sensor 104 with the branch limit. When the measured branch current is above the branch limit, the edge controller 100 sends a reduced pilot command to at least one connector of the plurality, that is, an assigned limit lower than the limit previously assigned to that connector, and starts a verification interval. The reduced pilot command is the first stage of the response, because reducing current through the control pilot lets a vehicle taper its draw and lets the session continue, which is preferable to interrupting the power path.
50	
51	At an ordered contactor shedding step 210, the edge controller 100 determines whether the measured branch current remains above the branch limit after the reduced pilot command and after the verification interval has elapsed. The verification interval is long enough for a vehicle that honours the reduced pilot command to have acted on it. If the measured branch current has fallen below the branch limit within the verification interval, the reduced pilot command has been effective and the edge controller 100 returns to the allocation interval process. If the measured branch current remains above the branch limit at the end of the verification interval, the pilot signalling has not produced the required reduction, and the edge controller 100 opens the connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch limit.
52	
53	The shedding order is stored in the nonvolatile memory 132 and defines the sequence in which the contactors of the plurality of connector stations are opened. The shedding order may be configured at installation, may be arranged so that the most recently started session is opened first, or may be arranged so that the session with the smallest energy-deficit value is opened first, so that the session that has already been served most is the one that gives up its power path. Opening the contactors one at a time, with the measured branch current re-evaluated between openings, removes only as much load as the measurement shows to be necessary: as soon as the measured branch current is below the branch limit, no further contactor is opened, and the remaining sessions continue.
54	
55	The staged sequence of a reduced pilot command, a verification interval, and then ordered interruption of the power path addresses the technical problem set out in the background. A control-pilot command is advisory, and a vehicle that ignores it, responds too slowly, or responds only in coarse steps leaves the branch loaded above its limit. Allocation that works only from commanded values cannot detect that condition at all. By taking the measured branch current from a sensor that is upstream of every connector contactor, and by treating the persistence of an over-limit measurement through a verification interval as the trigger for opening the power path, the edge controller 100 bounds the branch current with an action that is entirely within its own control, while still giving the cooperative case the opportunity to resolve without interrupting any session.
56	
57	Recovery after shedding
58	
59	At a reclose permissive step 212, the edge controller 100 governs the reclosing of a contactor that has been opened by the ordered contactor shedding step 210. The edge controller 100 does not reclose such a contactor until three conditions are satisfied together: the connector current sensor of that connector reports zero current, the control-pilot interface of that connector reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.
60	
61	Each condition addresses a distinct hazard. A report of zero current from the connector current sensor establishes that the power path is in fact open, so that a reclose command is not issued onto a path that is still carrying current. A report of a connected vehicle from the control-pilot interface establishes that there is a session to restore, so that the power path is not energized to a coupling from which the vehicle has been removed. The randomized recovery delay separates in time the reclosing of the contactors that were shed together, and separates the recovery of the equipment from the recovery of other equipment responding to the same site event, so that the loads do not return in unison and reproduce the overload that the shedding sequence has just relieved. The randomized recovery delay is drawn afresh for each contactor from a configured range, so that two contactors of the plurality do not become synchronized across successive events.
62	
63	On reclosing, the edge controller 100 resumes the allocation interval process, and the reclosed session takes part in the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202 and the deficit-based distribution step 204 in the ordinary way.
64	
65	Welded-contactor isolation
66	
67	At a welded-contactor isolation step 214, the edge controller 100 records a welded-contactor condition for a connector when the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector. The leakage threshold is a stored current magnitude above zero, chosen to be above the residual measurement that the connector current sensor reports on an open path and below any current that would represent load, so that sensor noise and standing offsets are not mistaken for a welded contact.
68	
69	When the welded-contactor condition has been recorded, the edge controller 100 inhibits the other contactors on the same branch and operates the local fault indicator 134. The other contactors are inhibited because a welded contactor consumes branch capacity that neither the allocation process nor the shedding sequence can recover: the shedding sequence believes that opening that contactor has released the current of that connector, and any further allocation made on that belief would overcommit the branch. Inhibiting the other contactors removes the controllable load from the branch and leaves only the current of the welded connector, which is the safe state available to the edge controller 100 with the means at its disposal. The local fault indicator 134 is operated at the equipment because the condition requires physical service and because it must be annunciated whether or not the network interface 108 is available.
70	
71	Operation during a network outage
72	
73	The edge controller 100 can receive remote schedules and authorizations through the network interface 108. A remote schedule may set the branch limit for a period of the day, and a remote authorization may permit a session at a given connector.
74	
75	The edge controller 100 stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in the nonvolatile memory 132. The signed local authorization token is issued by the remote management system, carries a cryptographic signature that the edge controller 100 verifies against a stored key, identifies the connectors it authorizes by their local connector identifiers, and carries an expiry. The last accepted branch limit is the most recent branch limit that the edge controller 100 has accepted from the remote management system.
76	
77	During a network outage the edge controller 100 continues already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and the independent branch-current safety process described above. Charging therefore continues through the outage, and continues within a limit that a responsible authority has set, rather than within a limit chosen locally because no other limit is available. The edge controller 100 does not start a newly connected session unless the signed local authorization token authorizes that connector and has not expired. A newly connected vehicle at a connector that the token does not authorize, or a newly connected vehicle at any connector after the token has expired, is not started until communication returns and a fresh authorization is obtained.
78	
79	Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence held in the nonvolatile memory 132. Each record is appended to the sequence together with a value computed over that record and over the preceding entry of the sequence, so that removal, reordering, or alteration of an entry is detectable from the sequence itself. The records accumulated during the outage are uploaded when communication returns, and the sequence values are uploaded with them, so that the remote management system can confirm that the uploaded run is complete and unaltered.
80	
81	Installation mapping through the service input
82	
83	A multi-connector installation is wired by hand, and the identifier a connector is given in configuration must correspond to the physical contactor and the physical current sensor channel that serve that connector. A transposition assigns a current limit intended for one connector to another. Every component continues to function, every sensor continues to report, and the allocation nevertheless governs the wrong power path.
84	
85	The service input 136 permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors. With the edge controller 100 in the commissioning mode entered through the service input 136, the edge controller 100 commands one low-energy pilot transition at a time, that is, it drives a pilot transition at a single connector, and confirms the corresponding connector current sensor by observing which sensed channel responds to that transition. The transition is a low-energy one, sufficient to produce a distinguishable response at the connector current sensor of the connector that is actually being driven, and the transitions are commanded one at a time so that the responding channel is unambiguous.
86	
87	The association between a connector identifier and a physical contactor is stored in the nonvolatile memory 132 only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector. If the responding channel is not the channel expected for the commanded connector, or if no channel responds, no association is stored for that connector. The mapping is thus established by measurement on the same sensors that the allocation process later relies upon, so a wiring-map error is found at commissioning instead of silently misdirecting current limits for the life of the installation.
88	
89	General considerations
90	
91	The allocation process, the branch protection process, the offline authorization behaviour, the welded-contactor isolation, and the installation mapping are described together because they share the sensors and the isolated local bus 106 of a single edge controller 100. They are nevertheless separable. An embodiment may carry out the allocation and branch protection processes without the offline authorization behaviour, without the tamper-evident record sequence, or without the commissioning mode, and an embodiment may include any combination of those additional features.
92	
93	The processes described above may be embodied as instructions stored on a non-transitory computer-readable medium and executed by the processing circuit 130. The values described as stored, including the branch limit, the configurable safety reserve, the minimum sustaining current, the shedding order, the leakage threshold, the range of the randomized recovery delay, the length of the allocation interval, and the length of the verification interval, may be configured at installation, may be set through the network interface 108, or may be held as defaults in the nonvolatile memory 132.
94	
95	The terms first and second are used to distinguish one connector station of the plurality from another and do not imply an order of importance or of operation. The system is not limited to two connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each connector station of the plurality. The embodiments described here are illustrative, and a person skilled in the art will recognize that elements described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with elements described in connection with another. The scope of the invention is defined by the claims that follow.
96

The first connector current sensor 122 measures the connector current flowing in that power path, that is, the current actually drawn by the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126.

The first control-pilot interface 124 presents a control-pilot signal to the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The control-pilot signal advertises a maximum current, called here the assigned limit, that the vehicle is permitted to draw, and reports the state of the coupling, including whether a vehicle is connected and whether that vehicle is requesting energy. The first control-pilot interface 124 therefore serves both as the command path by which an assigned limit reaches the vehicle and as a status path by which the presence of a connected vehicle is reported to the edge controller 100.

Each connector station of the plurality further has a local connector identifier. The local connector identifier is a stored value that distinguishes one connector of the plurality from another in the records, authorizations, and assignments held by the edge controller 100. The local connector identifier is a data value and does not appear as an inscription on the connector station in the drawings.

The distinction between the first control-pilot interface 124 and the first connector current sensor 122 is used throughout this description. The first control-pilot interface 124 carries a command. The first connector current sensor 122 carries a measurement. The edge controller 100 does not treat the assigned limit sent through the first control-pilot interface 124 as evidence of the current that the connector is drawing. It obtains that evidence from the first connector current sensor 122.

The edge controller

FIG. 3 shows the edge controller 100 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The edge controller 100 comprises a processing circuit 130 and a nonvolatile memory 132, and is coupled to the isolated local bus 106 and to the network interface 108. The processing circuit 130 may be a microcontroller, a microprocessor with associated volatile memory, a system on a chip, a programmable logic device, or a combination of such devices, and executes the allocation and protection processes described below. The nonvolatile memory 132 retains stored values across loss of supply, and may be flash memory, electrically erasable programmable read-only memory, ferroelectric memory, or another non-volatile storage device.

The edge controller 100 further comprises a local fault indicator 134 and a service input 136. The local fault indicator 134 provides an indication at the equipment itself, independently of the network interface 108, and may be a lamp, an illuminated legend, a display element, or an audible annunciator. The service input 136 is an input by which an installer places the edge controller 100 in a commissioning mode, and may be a physical control on the equipment, a locally connected service terminal, or a maintenance port that requires physical access to the enclosure of the edge controller 100.

For each active connector of the plurality, the edge controller 100 stores a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. The charging authorization records that the session at that connector is permitted to draw energy. The requested current is the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained, and may be obtained from the vehicle by way of the control-pilot interface of that connector, from the rating of the connector, or from a stored session parameter. The minimum sustaining current is the smallest assigned limit at which the session at that connector is expected to remain charging rather than terminating and requiring a new start, and may be a value that is common to the plurality of connectors or a value stored for each connector individually. The energy-deficit value represents the extent to which the session at that connector has been served less than its requested current over the shared-capacity period. In some implementations the energy-deficit value is accumulated over successive allocation intervals from the difference between the requested current of the session and the current assigned to that session. In other implementations the energy-deficit value is accumulated from the difference between the requested current and the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector, which additionally accounts for a vehicle that draws less than it was permitted to draw. In further implementations the energy-deficit value is derived from a stored energy target for the session and the energy delivered to that session so far. Any of these implementations gives a value that increases while a session is held below its request and decreases as the shortfall is made up, and the allocation process described below uses only that property of the value.

Allocation at each allocation interval

FIG. 4 shows the process carried out by the edge controller 100. The edge controller 100 repeats the allocation portion of the process at each allocation interval. The allocation interval is a recurring period, and its length is chosen so that assigned limits are revised more often than the load on the branch is expected to change materially, while remaining long enough for a vehicle to act on a previously assigned limit.

At an available-charging-current determination step 200, the edge controller 100 subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. The measured non-charging branch load is obtained from the branch current sensor 104 and the connector current sensors: the edge controller 100 takes the difference between the measured branch current and the sum of the connector currents measured at the connector stations, so that the portion of the branch current drawn by the non-charging load 114 is determined by measurement rather than by assumption. The configurable safety reserve is a stored margin that is withheld from allocation, and accommodates the measurement tolerance of the sensors, the step size and settling behaviour of vehicles responding to a changed assigned limit, and any increase in the non-charging load 114 that occurs between allocation intervals. Because the non-charging portion of the branch load is measured at each allocation interval and subtracted at the determination step 200, the available charging current follows the varying load of the site, and capacity released by the non-charging load 114 becomes available to the connectors instead of being permanently withheld.

At a minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, the edge controller 100 first assigns the minimum sustaining current to the sessions that can receive it. The edge controller 100 takes the active connectors in turn and assigns the minimum sustaining current of each to that connector for as long as the available charging current has not been exhausted. A session for which a remaining part of the available charging current at that allocation interval is less than its minimum sustaining current cannot receive the minimum sustaining current, and is assigned no current at that allocation interval rather than being assigned a value below its minimum sustaining current. Assigning a value below the minimum sustaining current would be worse than assigning nothing, because the session would be likely to terminate while still consuming allocated capacity, and would then require a new start. Where the available charging current is insufficient for every active session to receive its minimum sustaining current, the edge controller 100 selects the sessions to be sustained in order of energy deficit, so that the sessions that have been served least are sustained first.

At a deficit-based distribution step 204, the edge controller 100 distributes the remaining portion of the available charging current, that is, the portion left after the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, according to energy deficit. Sessions with a greater energy-deficit value receive a greater share of the remaining current than sessions with a smaller energy-deficit value. The distribution may be made in proportion to the energy-deficit values of the sessions, or by allocating to the session with the greatest energy-deficit value until its energy-deficit value falls to that of the next session and then allocating to those sessions together, or by another rule that orders the shares by energy deficit. No session is assigned more than its requested current, and any current that remains after every session has reached its requested current is left unassigned and is therefore added to the margin held on the branch. Distributing by energy deficit rather than by instantaneous request corrects, rather than perpetuates, the inequality that arises when one session begins while the branch is heavily loaded and another begins while it is lightly loaded.

At a limit transmission and connector current verification step 206, the edge controller 100 sends each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector, and then verifies the resulting connector current with the connector current sensor of that connector. Verification comprises comparing the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of a connector with the assigned limit sent to that connector. Where the measured connector current exceeds the assigned limit of that connector, the connector is not honouring the command it has been given, and the edge controller 100 records the deviation for that connector and treats the measured connector current, rather than the assigned limit, as the load that the connector places on the branch at the next allocation interval. The allocation is in this way closed loop at each connector: a connector that draws less than it has been permitted does not cause capacity to be withheld from the others, and a connector that draws more than it has been permitted does not cause the branch to be overcommitted at the next interval.

The branch current sensor as an independent safety input

The branch current sensor 104 is an independent safety input. It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the determination step 200: it governs a protection process that acts on the power path and that does not depend on the cooperation of any vehicle. The protection process is described with continued reference to FIG. 4.

At a pilot reduction step 208, the edge controller 100 compares the measured branch current from the branch current sensor 104 with the branch limit. When the measured branch current is above the branch limit, the edge controller 100 sends a reduced pilot command to at least one connector of the plurality, that is, an assigned limit lower than the limit previously assigned to that connector, and starts a verification interval. The reduced pilot command is the first stage of the response, because reducing current through the control pilot lets a vehicle taper its draw and lets the session continue, which is preferable to interrupting the power path.

At an ordered contactor shedding step 210, the edge controller 100 determines whether the measured branch current remains above the branch limit after the reduced pilot command and after the verification interval has elapsed. The verification interval is long enough for a vehicle that honours the reduced pilot command to have acted on it. If the measured branch current has fallen below the branch limit within the verification interval, the reduced pilot command has been effective and the edge controller 100 returns to the allocation interval process. If the measured branch current remains above the branch limit at the end of the verification interval, the pilot signalling has not produced the required reduction, and the edge controller 100 opens the connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch limit.

The shedding order is stored in the nonvolatile memory 132 and defines the sequence in which the contactors of the plurality of connector stations are opened. A control-pilot command is advisory, and a vehicle that ignores it, responds too slowly, or responds only in coarse steps leaves the branch loaded above its limit. Allocation that works only from commanded values cannot detect that condition at all. By taking the measured branch current from a sensor that is upstream of every connector contactor, and by treating the persistence of an over-limit measurement through a verification interval as the trigger for opening the power path, the edge controller 100 bounds the branch current with an action that is entirely within its own control, while still giving the cooperative case the opportunity to resolve without interrupting any session.

Recovery after shedding

At a reclose permissive step 212, the edge controller 100 governs the reclosing of a contactor that has been opened by the ordered contactor shedding step 210. The edge controller 100 does not reclose such a contactor until three conditions are satisfied together: the connector current sensor of that connector reports zero current, the control-pilot interface of that connector reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.

Each condition addresses a distinct hazard. A report of zero current from the connector current sensor establishes that the power path is in fact open, so that a reclose command is not issued onto a path that is still carrying current. A report of a connected vehicle from the control-pilot interface establishes that there is a session to restore, so that the power path is not energized to a coupling from which the vehicle has been removed. The randomized recovery delay separates in time the reclosing of the contactors that were shed together, and separates the recovery of the equipment from the recovery of other equipment responding to the same site event, so that the loads do not return in unison and reproduce the overload that the shedding sequence has just relieved. The randomized recovery delay is drawn afresh for each contactor from a configured range, so that two contactors of the plurality do not become synchronized across successive events.

On reclosing, the edge controller 100 resumes the allocation interval process, and the reclosed session takes part in the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202 and the deficit-based distribution step 204 in the ordinary way.

Welded-contactor isolation

At a welded-contactor isolation step 214, the edge controller 100 records a welded-contactor condition for a connector when the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector. The leakage threshold is a stored current magnitude above zero, chosen to be above the residual measurement that the connector current sensor reports on an open path and below any current that would represent load, so that sensor noise and standing offsets are not mistaken for a welded contact.

When the welded-contactor condition has been recorded, the edge controller 100 inhibits the other contactors on the same branch and operates the local fault indicator 134. The other contactors are inhibited because a welded contactor consumes branch capacity that neither the allocation process nor the shedding sequence can recover: the shedding sequence believes that opening that contactor has released the current of that connector, and any further allocation made on that belief would overcommit the branch. Inhibiting the other contactors removes the controllable load from the branch and leaves only the current of the welded connector, which is the safe state available to the edge controller 100 with the means at its disposal. The local fault indicator 134 is operated at the equipment because the condition requires physical service and because it must be annunciated whether or not the network interface 108 is available.

Operation during a network outage

The edge controller 100 can receive remote schedules and authorizations through the network interface 108. A remote schedule may set the branch limit for a period of the day, and a remote authorization may permit a session at a given connector.

The edge controller 100 stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in the nonvolatile memory 132. The signed local authorization token is issued by the remote management system, carries a cryptographic signature that the edge controller 100 verifies against a stored key, identifies the connectors it authorizes by their local connector identifiers, and carries an expiry. The last accepted branch limit is the most recent branch limit that the edge controller 100 has accepted from the remote management system.

During a network outage the edge controller 100 continues already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and the independent branch-current safety process described above. Charging therefore continues through the outage, and continues within a limit that a responsible authority has set, rather than within a limit chosen locally because no other limit is available. The edge controller 100 does not start a newly connected session unless the signed local authorization token authorizes that connector and has not expired. A newly connected vehicle at a connector that the token does not authorize, or a newly connected vehicle at any connector after the token has expired, is not started until communication returns and a fresh authorization is obtained.

Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence held in the nonvolatile memory 132. Each record is appended to the sequence together with a value computed over that record and over the preceding entry of the sequence, so that removal, reordering, or alteration of an entry is detectable from the sequence itself. The records accumulated during the outage are uploaded when communication returns, and the sequence values are uploaded with them, so that the remote management system can confirm that the uploaded run is complete and unaltered.

Installation mapping through the service input

A multi-connector installation is wired by hand, and the identifier a connector is given in configuration must correspond to the physical contactor and the physical current sensor channel that serve that connector. A transposition assigns a current limit intended for one connector to another. Every component continues to function, every sensor continues to report, and the allocation nevertheless governs the wrong power path.

The service input 136 permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors. With the edge controller 100 in the commissioning mode entered through the service input 136, the edge controller 100 commands one low-energy pilot transition at a time, that is, it drives a pilot transition at a single connector, and confirms the corresponding connector current sensor by observing which sensed channel responds to that transition. The transition is a low-energy one, sufficient to produce a distinguishable response at the connector current sensor of the connector that is actually being driven, and the transitions are commanded one at a time so that the responding channel is unambiguous.

The association between a connector identifier and a physical contactor is stored in the nonvolatile memory 132 only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector. If the responding channel is not the channel expected for the commanded connector, or if no channel responds, no association is stored for that connector. The mapping is thus established by measurement on the same sensors that the allocation process later relies upon, so a wiring-map error is found at commissioning instead of silently misdirecting current limits for the life of the installation.

General considerations

The allocation process, the branch protection process, the offline authorization behaviour, the welded-contactor isolation, and the installation mapping are described together because they share the sensors and the isolated local bus 106 of a single edge controller 100. They are nevertheless separable. An embodiment may carry out the allocation and branch protection processes without the offline authorization behaviour, without the tamper-evident record sequence, or without the commissioning mode, and an embodiment may include any combination of those additional features.

The processes described above may be embodied as instructions stored on a non-transitory computer-readable medium and executed by the processing circuit 130. The values described as stored, including the branch limit, the configurable safety reserve, the minimum sustaining current, the shedding order, the leakage threshold, the range of the randomized recovery delay, the length of the allocation interval, and the length of the verification interval, may be configured at installation, may be set through the network interface 108, or may be held as defaults in the nonvolatile memory 132.

The terms first and second are used to distinguish one connector station of the plurality from another and do not imply an order of importance or of operation. The system is not limited to two connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each connector station of the plurality. The embodiments described here are illustrative, and a person skilled in the art will recognize that elements described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with elements described in connection with another. The scope of the invention is defined by the claims that follow.

Recovery after shedding

At a reclose permissive step 212, the edge controller 100 governs the reclosing of a contactor that has been opened by the ordered contactor shedding step 210. The edge controller 100 does not reclose such a contactor until three conditions are satisfied together: the connector current sensor of that connector reports zero current, the control-pilot interface of that connector reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.

Each condition addresses a distinct hazard. A report of zero current from the connector current sensor establishes that the power path is in fact open, so that a reclose command is not issued onto a path that is still carrying current. A report of a connected vehicle from the control-pilot interface establishes that there is a session to restore, so that the power path is not energized to a coupling from which the vehicle has been removed. The randomized recovery delay separates in time the reclosing of the contactors that were shed together, and separates the recovery of the equipment from the recovery of other equipment responding to the same site event, so that the loads do not return in unison and reproduce the overload that the shedding sequence has just relieved. The randomized recovery delay is drawn afresh for each contactor from a configured range, so that two contactors of the plurality do not become synchronized across successive events.

On reclosing, the edge controller 100 resumes the allocation interval process, and the reclosed session takes part in the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202 and the deficit-based distribution step 204 in the ordinary way.

At a welded-contactor isolation step 214, the edge controller 100 records a welded-contactor condition for a connector when the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector. The leakage threshold is a stored current magnitude above zero, chosen to be above the residual measurement that the connector current sensor reports on an open path and below any current that would represent load, so that sensor noise and standing offsets are not mistaken for a welded contact.

The other contactors are inhibited because a welded contactor consumes branch capacity that neither the allocation process nor the shedding sequence can recover: the shedding sequence believes that opening that contactor has released the current of that connector, and any further allocation made on that belief would overcommit the branch. Inhibiting the other contactors removes the controllable load from the branch and leaves only the current of the welded connector, which is the safe state available to the edge controller 100 with the means at its disposal. The local fault indicator 134 is operated at the equipment because the condition requires physical service and because it must be annunciated whether or not the network interface 108 is available.

The edge controller 100 can receive remote schedules and authorizations through the network interface 108. A remote schedule may set the branch limit for a period of the day, and a remote authorization may permit a session at a given connector.

A newly connected vehicle at a connector that the token does not authorize, or a newly connected vehicle at any connector after the token has expired, is not started until communication returns and a fresh authorization is obtained.

Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence held in the nonvolatile memory 132. Each record is appended to the sequence together with a value computed over that record and over the preceding entry of the sequence, so that removal, reordering, or alteration of an entry is detectable from the sequence itself. In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part of this disclosure and show particular embodiments by way of illustration. Other embodiments may be used and structural or logical changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views.

Overview of the system

FIG. 1 shows a charging control system in which an edge controller 100 manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch. A branch conductor 102 supplies the plurality of connectors from a single point of protection. The allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, referred to in this description as the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors that the branch conductor 102 supplies. The branch limit is a stored value that corresponds to the aggregate current the branch is permitted to carry.

The branch conductor 102 supplies a first connector station 110 and a second connector station 112. Two connector stations are shown for clarity of illustration. The system accommodates a larger plurality of connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each further connector station of the plurality. The branch conductor 102 also supplies a non-charging load 114, which represents lighting, building services, and other equipment that is connected to the same branch and that is not under the control of the edge controller 100.

A branch current sensor 104 measures total current on the branch conductor 102 upstream of the contactors of the connector stations. Because the branch current sensor 104 is located upstream of those contactors, the current it measures includes both the current drawn by the connector stations and the current drawn by the non-charging load 114. The branch current sensor 104 may be a current transformer, a Rogowski coil, a Hall-effect sensor, a shunt with an isolated amplifier, or another transducer that reports the magnitude of alternating current on a conductor. Where the branch is polyphase, the branch current sensor 104 comprises a transducer for each phase conductor of the branch, and measured branch current is taken as the greatest of the per-phase magnitudes, so that the branch limit governs the most heavily loaded phase.

The edge controller 100 communicates with the connector stations over an isolated local bus 106. The isolated local bus 106 carries assigned current limits and contactor commands from the edge controller 100 to the connector stations, and carries connector current measurements and control-pilot status from the connector stations to the edge controller 100. The isolated local bus 106 provides galvanic isolation between the edge controller 100 and the signalling electronics of each connector station, so that a fault in the power path of one connector station is not communicated to the edge controller 100 or to the remaining connector stations. The isolated local bus 106 may be implemented as a differential serial bus with isolated transceivers at each node, as a set of point-to-point isolated links, or as an optically isolated bus, and its physical form is not essential to the operation described here.

A network interface 108 connects the edge controller 100 to a remote management system. The network interface 108 may be a wired network port, a cellular modem, or a wireless network interface. As described below, the network interface 108 conveys remote schedules and authorizations to the edge controller 100 and conveys uploaded meter records from the edge controller 100, but the safety behaviour of the system does not depend on the availability of the network interface 108.

The connector station

FIG. 2 shows the first connector station 110 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The first connector station 110 comprises a first contactor 120, a first connector current sensor 122, a first control-pilot interface 124, and a first vehicle connector 126. The first contactor 120 is connected in the power path between the branch conductor 102 and the first vehicle connector 126 and, when closed, permits current to flow from the branch conductor 102 to a vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The first connector current sensor 122 measures the connector current flowing in that power path, that is, the current actually drawn by the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126.

The first control-pilot interface 124 presents a control-pilot signal to the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The control-pilot signal advertises a maximum current, called here the assigned limit, that the vehicle is permitted to draw, and reports the state of the coupling, including whether a vehicle is connected and whether that vehicle is requesting energy. The first control-pilot interface 124 therefore serves both as the command path by which an assigned limit reaches the vehicle and as a status path by which the presence of a connected vehicle is reported to the edge controller 100.

Each connector station of the plurality further has a local connector identifier. The local connector identifier is a stored value that distinguishes one connector of the plurality from another in the records, authorizations, and assignments held by the edge controller 100. The local connector identifier is a data value and does not appear as an inscription on the connector station in the drawings.

The distinction between the first control-pilot interface 124 and the first connector current sensor 122 is used throughout this description. The first control-pilot interface 124 carries a command. The first connector current sensor 122 carries a measurement. The edge controller 100 does not treat the assigned limit sent through the first control-pilot interface 124 as evidence of the current that the connector is drawing. It obtains that evidence from the first connector current sensor 122.

FIG. 3 shows the edge controller 100 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The edge controller 100 comprises a processing circuit 130 and a nonvolatile memory 132, and is coupled to the isolated local bus 106 and to the network interface 108. The processing circuit 130 may be a microcontroller, a microprocessor with associated volatile memory, a system on a chip, a programmable logic device, or a combination of such devices, and executes the allocation and protection processes described below. The nonvolatile memory 132 retains stored values across loss of supply, and may be flash memory, electrically erasable programmable read-only memory, ferroelectric memory, or another non-volatile storage device.

The edge controller 100 further comprises a local fault indicator 134 and a service input 136. The local fault indicator 134 provides an indication at the equipment itself, independently of the network interface 108, and may be a lamp, an illuminated legend, a display element, or an audible annunciator. The service input 136 is an input by which an installer places the edge controller 100 in a commissioning mode, and may be a physical control on the equipment, a locally connected service terminal, or a maintenance port that requires physical access to the enclosure of the edge controller 100.

For each active connector of the plurality, the edge controller 100 stores a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. The charging authorization records that the session at that connector is permitted to draw energy. The requested current is the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained, and may be obtained from the vehicle by way of the control-pilot interface of that connector, from the rating of the connector, or from a stored session parameter. The minimum sustaining current is the smallest assigned limit at which the session at that connector is expected to remain charging rather than terminating and requiring a new start, and may be a value that is common to the plurality of connectors or a value stored for each connector individually. The energy-deficit value represents the extent to which the session at that connector has been served less than its requested current over the shared-capacity period. In some implementations the energy-deficit value is accumulated over successive allocation intervals from the difference between the requested current of the session and the current assigned to that session. In other implementations the energy-deficit value is accumulated from the difference between the requested current and the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector, which additionally accounts for a vehicle that draws less than it was permitted to draw. In further implementations the energy-deficit value is derived from a stored energy target for the session and the energy delivered to that session so far. Any of these implementations gives a value that increases while a session is held below its request and decreases as the shortfall is made up, and the allocation process described below uses only that property of the value.
