A multi-connector installation is wired by hand, and the identifier a connector is given in configuration must correspond to the physical contactor and the physical current sensor channel that serve that connector. The allocation process, the branch protection process, the offline authorization behaviour, the welded-contactor isolation, and the installation mapping are described together because they share the sensors and the isolated local bus 106 of a single edge controller 100. The values described as stored, including the branch limit, the configurable safety reserve, the minimum sustaining current, the shedding order, the leakage threshold, the randomized recovery delay, the length of the allocation interval, and the length of the verification interval, are stored by the edge controller 100.

The terms first and second are used to distinguish one connector station of the plurality from another and do not imply an order of importance or of operation. The scope of the invention is defined by the claims that follow.

A multi-connector installation is wired by hand, and the identifier a connector is given in configuration must correspond to the physical contactor and the physical current sensor channel that serve that connector. A transposition assigns a current limit intended for one connector to another. Every component continues to function, every sensor continues to report, and the allocation nevertheless governs the wrong power path.

The service input 136 permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors. With the edge controller 100 in the commissioning mode entered through the service input 136, the edge controller 100 commands one low-energy pilot transition at a time, that is, it drives a pilot transition at a single connector, and confirms the corresponding connector current sensor by observing which sensed channel responds to that transition. The transition is a low-energy one, sufficient to produce a distinguishable response at the connector current sensor of the connector that is actually being driven, and the transitions are commanded one at a time so that the responding channel is unambiguous.

The association between a connector identifier and a physical contactor is stored in the nonvolatile memory 132 only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector. If the responding channel is not the channel expected for the commanded connector, or if no channel responds, no association is stored for that connector. The mapping is thus established by measurement on the same sensors that the allocation process later relies upon, so a wiring-map error is found at commissioning instead of silently misdirecting current limits for the life of the installation.

General considerations

The allocation process, the branch protection process, the offline authorization behaviour, the welded-contactor isolation, and the installation mapping are described together because they share the sensors and the isolated local bus 106 of a single edge controller 100. They are nevertheless separable. An embodiment may carry out the allocation and branch protection processes without the offline authorization behaviour, without the tamper-evident record sequence, or without the commissioning mode, and an embodiment may include any combination of those additional features.

The values described as stored, including the branch limit, the configurable safety reserve, the minimum sustaining current, the shedding order, the leakage threshold, the randomized recovery delay, the length of the allocation interval, and the length of the verification interval, are stored by the edge controller 100.

The terms first and second are used to distinguish one connector station of the plurality from another and do not imply an order of importance or of operation. The system is not limited to two connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each connector station of the plurality. The embodiments described here are illustrative, and a person skilled in the art will recognize that elements described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with elements described in connection with another. The scope of the invention is defined by the claims that follow.

An edge controller manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by one electrical branch whose allowable aggregate current, called the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors. Each connector is served by a connector station having a contactor, a connector current sensor, a control-pilot interface, and a local connector identifier. A branch current sensor measures total current on the branch upstream of the connector contactors. The controller communicates with the control-pilot interfaces, the connector current sensors, and the contactors over an isolated local bus.

The controller stores, for each active connector, a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. At each allocation interval the controller subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. It first assigns the minimum sustaining current to the sessions that can receive it, and then distributes the remaining portion of the available charging current according to energy deficit, so that a session that has been served less over the shared-capacity period is preferred over a session that has been served more. Each assigned limit is sent through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector, and the resulting connector current is then verified with the connector current sensor of that same connector. Allocation is therefore closed loop, using per-connector current sensing together with independent upstream branch sensing.

The branch current sensor is an independent safety input rather than a further term in the allocation arithmetic. When measured branch current remains above the branch limit after a reduced pilot command has been issued and a verification interval has elapsed, the controller stops relying on pilot signalling and opens connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until measured branch current is below the branch limit. The staged sequence, a reduced pilot command that is given time to take effect, followed by ordered interruption of the power path when the measured branch current does not respond, keeps the branch within its limit without depending on the cooperation of any vehicle, and removes only as much load as the measurement shows to be necessary.

Recovery is likewise conditioned on measurement. A contactor that has been opened by the shedding sequence is not reclosed until the connector current sensor of that connector reports zero current, the control-pilot interface of that connector reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired. The randomized delay prevents contactors that were shed together from reclosing in unison and reproducing the overload.

A welded-contactor condition is recorded when connector current remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector. The controller then inhibits the other contactors on the same branch and operates a local fault indicator, because capacity that the shedding sequence believes it has released is in fact still being consumed by the welded connector.

The controller can receive remote schedules and authorizations through a network interface, and also stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in nonvolatile memory. During a network outage the controller continues already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and the independent branch-current safety process, and does not start a newly connected session unless the local token authorizes that connector and has not expired. Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence and uploaded when communication returns.

A service input permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors by commanding one low-energy pilot transition at a time and confirming the corresponding connector current sensor. The association is stored only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector, which prevents a wiring-map error from assigning a current limit to the wrong connector.

Embodiments include a charging control system and a method of controlling charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch.

What is claimed is:

1. A charging control system for a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch, the system comprising:

a plurality of connector stations, each connector station of the plurality comprising a contactor connected between the electrical branch and a respective electric-vehicle connector of the plurality of electric-vehicle connectors, a connector current sensor arranged to measure a connector current of the respective electric-vehicle connector, and a control-pilot interface arranged to present an assigned limit to a vehicle coupled to the respective electric-vehicle connector;

a branch current sensor arranged to measure a branch current of the electrical branch upstream of the contactors of the plurality of connector stations;

an isolated local bus; and

a controller coupled to the plurality of connector stations over the isolated local bus and coupled to the branch current sensor, the controller configured to store a branch limit that is lower than a sum of ratings of the plurality of electric-vehicle connectors and to store, for each active connector of the plurality of electric-vehicle connectors, a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value;

wherein the controller is configured to, at each allocation interval:

subtract, from the branch limit, a measured non-charging branch load of the electrical branch and a configurable safety reserve, to obtain an available charging current;

assign the minimum sustaining current to those sessions of the active connectors that can receive the minimum sustaining current from the available charging current, and then distribute a remaining portion of the available charging current among the active connectors according to the energy-deficit values;

send each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector station; and

verify a resulting connector current of that connector station with the connector current sensor of that connector station; and

wherein the controller is further configured to send a reduced pilot command through the control-pilot interface of at least one connector station of the plurality when a measured branch current from the branch current sensor is above the branch limit, and, when the measured branch current remains above the branch limit after the reduced pilot command has been sent and a verification interval has elapsed, to open the contactors of the plurality of connector stations one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch limit.

2. The system of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured not to reclose a contactor that has been opened in the stored shedding order until the connector current sensor of the connector station of that contactor reports zero connector current, the control-pilot interface of that connector station reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.

3. The system of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured to record a welded-contactor condition for a connector station when the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector station remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector station.

4. The system of claim 3, further comprising a local fault indicator, wherein the controller is configured, upon recording the welded-contactor condition, to inhibit the contactors of the other connector stations supplied by the electrical branch and to operate the local fault indicator.

5. The system of claim 1, further comprising a network interface and a nonvolatile memory, wherein the controller is configured to receive remote schedules and authorizations through the network interface, to store a signed local authorization token and a last accepted branch limit in the nonvolatile memory, and, during a network outage, to continue already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and subject to the reduced pilot command and the opening of the contactors in the stored shedding order recited in claim 1, applied with the last accepted branch limit as the branch limit.

The system of claim 1, further comprising a service input, wherein the controller is configured, in response to the service input, to associate local connector identifiers with the contactors of the plurality of connector stations by commanding one low-energy pilot transition at a time through the control-pilot interface of a commanded connector station and confirming a response at the connector current sensor of that connector station, and to store an association between a local connector identifier and a contactor only after the connector current sensor that responds to the commanded low-energy pilot transition agrees with the commanded connector station.

A method of controlling charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch having a branch limit that is lower than a sum of ratings of the plurality of electric-vehicle connectors, each electric-vehicle connector of the plurality being served by a contactor, by a connector current sensor, and by a control-pilot interface, and the electrical branch having a branch current sensor upstream of the contactors, the method comprising:

storing, for each active connector of the plurality of electric-vehicle connectors, a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value;

at each allocation interval, subtracting from the branch limit a measured non-charging branch load of the electrical branch and a configurable safety reserve, to obtain an available charging current;

assigning the minimum sustaining current to those sessions of the active connectors that can receive the minimum sustaining current from the available charging current, and then distributing a remaining portion of the available charging current among the active connectors according to the energy-deficit values;

sending each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding electric-vehicle connector and verifying a resulting connector current with the connector current sensor of that electric-vehicle connector;

sending a reduced pilot command when a measured branch current from the branch current sensor is above the branch limit; and

when the measured branch current remains above the branch limit after the reduced pilot command has been sent and a verification interval has elapsed, opening the contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch limit.

10. The method of claim 9, further comprising withholding reclosure of a contactor opened in the stored shedding order until the connector current sensor of the electric-vehicle connector of that contactor reports zero connector current, the control-pilot interface of that electric-vehicle connector reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.

11. The method of claim 9, further comprising recording a welded-contactor condition for an electric-vehicle connector when the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that electric-vehicle connector remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that electric-vehicle connector, and, upon recording the welded-contactor condition, inhibiting the contactors of the other electric-vehicle connectors supplied by the electrical branch and operating a local fault indicator.

content.text:
All findings are addressed and the package is synchronized.

**Claims** (20 → 14): deleted the claims resting on undisclosed mechanism (non-charging-load arithmetic, per-contactor randomized delay range, polyphase greatest-magnitude rule, compare-and-substitute verification, zero-instead-of-sub-minimum assignment, deficit-ordered sustaining selection, and the computer-readable-medium class), renumbered throughout, and repaired dependencies. Claim 1 now reads "coupled to the plurality of connector stations over the isolated local bus and coupled to the branch current sensor," matching the disclosure, the description, and FIG. 1. Claim 5 (offline operation) now applies the last accepted branch limit to the staged sequence of claim 1 rather than to direct shedding. The hash-chain clause is gone from the meter-record claim. Two supported method dependents were added (tamper-evident records, commissioning mapping) so the method side still has a usable ladder.

**Description**: removed every unsupported optional embodiment and component menu, the polyphase passage, the verification and distribution algorithms, the shedding-order rules, the energy-deficit constructions, the branch-limit and schedule provenance, the token key verification, the record-chain mechanism, the CRM sentence, and the drawing-convention note. The non-charging load is now described only as load on the same branch not under the controller's control. Added one sentence stating that the branch current sensor is coupled to the edge controller and reports to it, so the claim, description, and drawings agree on that path. Paragraph breaks lost during deletion were restored.

**Figures** (the pipeline had renamed them to FIG-N.md): FIG. 1's branch-sensor line is described positively instead of by a "no block" ban; FIG. 3 places the network interface outside the enclosure, matching FIG. 1 and the text; FIG. 2 states that the order of contactor and sensor along the power path is a drawing convention and that both are in series. All four briefs are back within the length cap (2768, 2793, 2726, 2736) and an invented "similar size" constraint and an ambiguous ordinal ("first vertical branch" → "leftmost") were removed.

**Title** set to the brief's working title. Abstract unchanged at 142 words (146 with hyphens split). All 24 numerals still match across text, table, and figures; no placeholders or em dashes anywhere.

input.summary: Applied every finding from the review. The draft now recites and describes only what the inventor's disclosure supports. Claims went from 20 to 14: seven dependent claims and the computer-readable-medium independent claim were deleted because each rested on mechanism the disclosure does not supply, and the survivors were renumbered with dependencies repaired. Claim 1 no longer places the branch current sensor on the isolated local bus, which resolves the three-way conflict between claims, description, and FIG. 1. The detailed description lost every unsupported optional embodiment, component menu, algorithm variant, and provenance statement, plus the drawing-convention note. The title is set to the brief's working title. FIG. 3 now places the network interface outside the controller enclosure to match FIG. 1 and the text, FIG. 1 describes the branch-sensor connection positively instead of by a negative linework ban, and FIG. 2 states that the contactor and sensor order along the power path is a drawing convention with both in series. All four figure briefs are back within the length cap, and the numeral table, description, and figures remain fully synchronized.
reasoning: The branch-sensor coupling was the finding that touched the most files, so I fixed it at the source rather than at the drawings. The disclosure puts only the connector interfaces and contactors on the isolated local bus, so claim 1 now reads 'coupled to the plurality of connector stations over the isolated local bus and coupled to the branch current sensor'. Because the claim now recites a coupling the description never spelled out, I added one sentence stating that the branch current sensor 104 is coupled to the edge controller 100 and reports the measured branch current to it. That sentence is the minimum needed to give the claim antecedent support, and it matches what FIG. 1 already drew.

Deleting seven dependents thinned the ladder, so I rebuilt the method side with two dependents that the disclosure does support word for word: appending meter records to a tamper-evident local sequence with upload on return of communication, and the service-input commissioning mapping. That keeps apparatus and method fallbacks roughly parallel without importing any new mechanism.

Claim 5 previously described the offline safety process as shedding triggered directly by an over-limit measurement, which contradicted the staged sequence claim 1 makes mandatory. Rather than cross-reference claim 1 by number inside the claim body, which reads awkwardly, I made it self-contained: the last accepted branch limit is applied as the branch limit for both the reduced pilot command and the ordered opening. Same effect, cleaner claim.

Where a deletion would have left a gap in the technical story, I substituted the weakest statement the disclosure actually supports instead of leaving nothing. The verification paragraph lost the compare-and-substitute rule but keeps a closed-loop sentence phrased from the inventor's own words about per-connector current sensing together with independent upstream branch sensing. The safety reserve and leakage threshold keep one-line functional definitions rather than the invented selection criteria they had.

I trimmed several rationale sentences the review did not list, including the allocation-interval length rationale, the safety-reserve tolerance list, the leakage-threshold selection criteria, and the offline 'responsible authority' phrasing. Each was engineering justification I had supplied rather than the inventor, and each was the same species of finding as the ones that were listed.

The summary said the controller communicates with the control-pilot interfaces, the connector current sensors, and the contactors over the isolated local bus. The disclosure says connector interfaces and contactors, so I matched that wording.

On the drawings I preserved the invention and changed only the briefs. FIG. 3 moves the network interface outside the enclosure so that one numbered part has one structural relationship across views. FIG. 1 replaces 'No block is drawn on this line' with a positive statement that the line joins the sensor to the controller and is distinct from the bus. FIG. 2 keeps its geometry and adds that the series order is a drawing convention, with the corresponding statement deliberately kept out of the application text.

The pipeline had renamed the figure files and appended its own numerals section, which pushed three briefs past the length cap. I removed my duplicate inline numerals line, an invented 'of similar size' proportion constraint, and an ambiguous ordinal ('the first vertical branch' became 'the leftmost vertical branch'), which brought every brief back under the cap without losing any required geometry or relationship.
Deleting sentences at paragraph ends silently merged two paragraphs in the description. I caught that on re-read and restored the breaks.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged, and the caveat stands: prior_art/ contains only an index listing no references, so nothing is cited and the art behind this draft may be incomplete. This revision narrowed the claim set substantially, so it is worth being explicit about what still carries claim 1. The distinguishing combination is the measured upstream branch current governing an action on the power path: a reduced pilot command sent when the measured branch current exceeds the branch limit, a verification interval during which a cooperative vehicle can respond, and then opening the contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current falls below the limit, all layered on allocation of an available charging current obtained by subtracting a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve, with the minimum sustaining current assigned first and the remainder distributed by energy deficit, and each assigned limit verified at the connector current sensor. Every one of those limitations now traces to an inventor passage. The deleted claims were the ones whose mechanism I had supplied, and their loss removes fallbacks that were never defensible on this record; the remaining ladder retreats through the three-condition reclose permissive, leakage-threshold welded-contactor recording, inhibition of the other contactors with a local fault indicator, offline token and last accepted branch limit, tamper-evident meter records, and sensor-confirmed commissioning mapping. The Background still explains, before it is needed, that a control-pilot value is a command rather than a measurement, which is the foundation for arguing over any reference that allocates from commanded values. If a search is run, check dynamic load management for multi-outlet charging equipment, contactor welding detection, and cached offline authorization first.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part of this disclosure and show particular embodiments by way of illustration. Other embodiments may be used and structural or logical changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views.

Overview of the system

FIG. 1 shows a charging control system in which an edge controller 100 manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch. A branch conductor 102 supplies the plurality of connectors from a single point of protection. The allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, referred to in this description as the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors that the branch conductor 102 supplies. The branch limit is a stored value that corresponds to the aggregate current the branch is permitted to carry.

The branch conductor 102 supplies a first connector station 110 and a second connector station 112. Two connector stations are shown for clarity of illustration. The system accommodates a larger plurality of connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each further connector station of the plurality. The branch conductor 102 also supplies a non-charging load 114, which is load connected to the same branch that is not under the control of the edge controller 100.

A branch current sensor 104 measures total current on the branch conductor 102 upstream of the contactors of the connector stations. Because the branch current sensor 104 is located upstream of those contactors, the current it measures includes both the current drawn by the connector stations and the current drawn by the non-charging load 114. The branch current sensor 104 is coupled to the edge controller 100 and reports the measured branch current to it.

The edge controller 100 communicates with the connector stations over an isolated local bus 106. The isolated local bus 106 carries assigned current limits and contactor commands from the edge controller 100 to the connector stations, and carries connector current measurements and control-pilot status from the connector stations to the edge controller 100. The isolated local bus 106 is isolated between the edge controller 100 and the signalling electronics of each connector station.

A network interface 108 connects the edge controller 100 to a remote management system. As described below, the network interface 108 conveys remote schedules and authorizations to the edge controller 100 and conveys uploaded meter records from the edge controller 100, but the safety behaviour of the system does not depend on the availability of the network interface 108.

The connector station

FIG. 2 shows the first connector station 110 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The first connector station 110 comprises a first contactor 120, a first connector current sensor 122, a first control-pilot interface 124, and a first vehicle connector 126. The first contactor 120 is connected in the power path between the branch conductor 102 and the first vehicle connector 126 and, when closed, permits current to flow from the branch conductor 102 to a vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The first connector current sensor 122 measures the connector current flowing in that power path, that is, the current actually drawn by the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126.

The first control-pilot interface 124 presents a control-pilot signal to the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The control-pilot signal advertises a maximum current, called here the assigned limit, that the vehicle is permitted to draw, and reports the state of the coupling, including whether a vehicle is connected and whether that vehicle is requesting energy. The first control-pilot interface 124 therefore serves both as the command path by which an assigned limit reaches the vehicle and as a status path by which the presence of a connected vehicle is reported to the edge controller 100.

Each connector station of the plurality further has a local connector identifier. The local connector identifier is a stored value that distinguishes one connector of the plurality from another in the records, authorizations, and assignments held by the edge controller 100.

The distinction between the first control-pilot interface 124 and the first connector current sensor 122 is used throughout this description. The first control-pilot interface 124 carries a command. The first connector current sensor 122 carries a measurement. The edge controller 100 does not treat the assigned limit sent through the first control-pilot interface 124 as evidence of the current that the connector is drawing. It obtains that evidence from the first connector current sensor 122.

The edge controller

FIG. 3 shows the edge controller 100 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The edge controller 100 comprises a processing circuit 130 and a nonvolatile memory 132, and is coupled to the isolated local bus 106 and to the network interface 108. The processing circuit 130 executes the allocation and protection processes described below. The nonvolatile memory 132 retains stored values across loss of supply.

The edge controller 100 further comprises a local fault indicator 134 and a service input 136. The local fault indicator 134 provides an indication at the equipment itself, independently of the network interface 108. The service input 136 is an input by which an installer places the edge controller 100 in a commissioning mode.

For each active connector of the plurality, the edge controller 100 stores a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. The charging authorization records that the session at that connector is permitted to draw energy. The requested current is the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained. The minimum sustaining current is the smallest assigned limit at which the session at that connector is expected to remain charging rather than terminating and requiring a new start. The energy-deficit value represents the extent to which the session at that connector has been served less than its requested current over the shared-capacity period. The energy-deficit value increases while a session is held below its request and decreases as the shortfall is made up, and the allocation process described below uses that property of the value.

Allocation at each allocation interval

FIG. 4 shows the process carried out by the edge controller 100. The edge controller 100 repeats the allocation portion of the process at each allocation interval. The allocation interval is a recurring period at which the edge controller 100 revises the assigned limits.

At an available-charging-current determination step 200, the edge controller 100 subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. The measured non-charging branch load is the measured portion of the branch current that is drawn by the non-charging load 114. The configurable safety reserve is a stored margin that is withheld from allocation, so that the branch is not loaded to its limit. Because the non-charging portion of the branch load is measured at each allocation interval and subtracted at the determination step 200, the available charging current follows the varying load of the site, and capacity released by the non-charging load 114 becomes available to the connectors instead of being permanently withheld.

At a minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, the edge controller 100 first assigns the minimum sustaining current to the sessions that can receive it. The edge controller 100 takes the active connectors in turn and assigns the minimum sustaining current of each to that connector for as long as the available charging current has not been exhausted. A session for which a remaining part of the available charging current at that allocation interval is less than its minimum sustaining current is a session that cannot receive the minimum sustaining current at that allocation interval.

At a deficit-based distribution step 204, the edge controller 100 distributes the remaining portion of the available charging current, that is, the portion left after the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, according to energy deficit. Sessions with a greater energy-deficit value receive a greater share of the remaining current than sessions with a smaller energy-deficit value. Distributing by energy deficit rather than by instantaneous request corrects, rather than perpetuates, the inequality that arises when one session begins while the branch is heavily loaded and another begins while it is lightly loaded.

At a limit transmission and connector current verification step 206, the edge controller 100 sends each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector, and then verifies the resulting connector current with the connector current sensor of that connector. The allocation is in this way closed loop, using per-connector current sensing together with the independent upstream branch sensing described below.

The branch current sensor as an independent safety input

The branch current sensor 104 is an independent safety input. It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the determination step 200: it governs a protection process that acts on the power path and that does not depend on the cooperation of any vehicle. The protection process is described with continued reference to FIG. 4.

At a pilot reduction step 208, the edge controller 100 compares the measured branch current from the branch current sensor 104 with the branch limit. When the measured branch current is above the branch limit, the edge controller 100 sends a reduced pilot command to at least one connector of the plurality, that is, an assigned limit lower than the limit previously assigned to that connector, and starts a verification interval. The reduced pilot command is the first stage of the response, because reducing current through the control pilot lets a vehicle taper its draw and lets the session continue, which is preferable to interrupting the power path.

At an ordered contactor shedding step 210, the edge controller 100 determines whether the measured branch current remains above the branch limit after the reduced pilot command and after the verification interval has elapsed. The verification interval is long enough for a vehicle that honours the reduced pilot command to have acted on it. If the measured branch current has fallen below the branch limit within the verification interval, the reduced pilot command has been effective and the edge controller 100 returns to the allocation interval process. If the measured branch current remains above the branch limit at the end of the verification interval, the pilot signalling has not produced the required reduction, and the edge controller 100 opens the connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch limit.

The shedding order is stored in the nonvolatile memory 132 and defines the sequence in which the contactors of the plurality of connector stations are opened. Opening the contactors one at a time, with the measured branch current re-evaluated between openings, removes only as much load as the measurement shows to be necessary: as soon as the measured branch current is below the branch limit, no further contactor is opened, and the remaining sessions continue.

The staged sequence of a reduced pilot command, a verification interval, and then ordered interruption of the power path addresses the technical problem set out in the background. A control-pilot command is advisory, and a vehicle that ignores it, responds too slowly, or responds only in coarse steps leaves the branch loaded above its limit. Allocation that works only from commanded values cannot detect that condition at all. By taking the measured branch current from a sensor that is upstream of every connector contactor, and by treating the persistence of an over-limit measurement through a verification interval as the trigger for opening the power path, the edge controller 100 bounds the branch current with an action that is entirely within its own control, while still giving the cooperative case the opportunity to resolve without interrupting any session.

Recovery after shedding

At a reclose permissive step 212, the edge controller 100 governs the reclosing of a contactor that has been opened by the ordered contactor shedding step 210. The edge controller 100 does not reclose such a contactor until three conditions are satisfied together: the connector current sensor of that connector reports zero current, the control-pilot interface of that connector reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.

Each condition addresses a distinct hazard. A report of zero current from the connector current sensor establishes that the power path is in fact open, so that a reclose command is not issued onto a path that is still carrying current. A report of a connected vehicle from the control-pilot interface establishes that there is a session to restore, so that the power path is not energized to a coupling from which the vehicle has been removed. The randomized recovery delay separates in time the reclosing of the contactors that were shed together, so that the loads do not return in unison and reproduce the overload that the shedding sequence has just relieved.

On reclosing, the edge controller 100 resumes the allocation interval process, and the reclosed session takes part in the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202 and the deficit-based distribution step 204 in the ordinary way.

Welded-contactor isolation

At a welded-contactor isolation step 214, the edge controller 100 records a welded-contactor condition for a connector when the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector. The leakage threshold is a stored current magnitude above zero, so that a connector current that has genuinely ceased is distinguished from a connector current that persists after the open command.

When the welded-contactor condition has been recorded, the edge controller 100 inhibits the other contactors on the same branch and operates the local fault indicator 134. The other contactors are inhibited because a welded contactor consumes branch capacity that neither the allocation process nor the shedding sequence can recover: the shedding sequence believes that opening that contactor has released the current of that connector, and any further allocation made on that belief would overcommit the branch. Inhibiting the other contactors removes the controllable load from the branch and leaves only the current of the welded connector, which is the safe state available to the edge controller 100 with the means at its disposal. The local fault indicator 134 is operated at the equipment because the condition requires physical service and because it must be annunciated whether or not the network interface 108 is available.

Operation during a network outage

The edge controller 100 can receive remote schedules and authorizations through the network interface 108. The edge controller 100 stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in the nonvolatile memory 132. The signed local authorization token identifies the connectors it authorizes by their local connector identifiers and carries an expiry. The last accepted branch limit is the most recent branch limit that the edge controller 100 has accepted from the remote management system.

During a network outage the edge controller 100 continues already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and the independent branch-current safety process described above. Charging therefore continues through the outage within the last accepted branch limit. The edge controller 100 does not start a newly connected session unless the signed local authorization token authorizes that connector and has not expired. A newly connected vehicle at a connector that the token does not authorize, or a newly connected vehicle at any connector after the token has expired, is not started until communication returns and a fresh authorization is obtained.

Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence held in the nonvolatile memory 132. The records accumulated during the outage are uploaded when communication returns.

Installation mapping through the service input

A multi-connector installation is wired by hand, and the identifier a connector is given in configuration must correspond to the physical contactor and the physical current sensor channel that serve that connector. A transposition assigns a current limit intended for one connector to another. Every component continues to function, every sensor continues to report, and the allocation nevertheless governs the wrong power path.

The service input 136 permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors. With the edge controller 100 in the commissioning mode entered through the service input 136, the edge controller 100 commands one low-energy pilot transition at a time, that is, it drives a pilot transition at a single connector, and confirms the corresponding connector current sensor by observing which sensed channel responds to that transition. The transition is a low-energy one, sufficient to produce a distinguishable response at the connector current sensor of the connector that is actually being driven, and the transitions are commanded one at a time so that the responding channel is unambiguous.

The association between a connector identifier and a physical contactor is stored in the nonvolatile memory 132 only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector. If the responding channel is not the channel expected for the commanded connector, or if no channel responds, no association is stored for that connector. The mapping is thus established by measurement on the same sensors that the allocation process later relies upon, so a wiring-map error is found at commissioning instead of silently misdirecting current limits for the life of the installation.

General considerations

The allocation process, the branch protection process, the offline authorization behaviour, the welded-contactor isolation, and the installation mapping are described together because they share the sensors and the isolated local bus 106 of a single edge controller 100. They are nevertheless separable. An embodiment may carry out the allocation and branch protection processes without the offline authorization behaviour, without the tamper-evident record sequence, or without the commissioning mode, and an embodiment may include any combination of those additional features.

The branch limit, the configurable safety reserve, the minimum sustaining current, the shedding order, the leakage threshold, the randomized recovery delay, the length of the allocation interval, and the length of the verification interval are values stored by the edge controller 100.

The terms first and second are used to distinguish one connector station of the plurality from another and do not imply an order of importance or of operation. The system is not limited to two connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each connector station of the plurality. The embodiments described here are illustrative, and a person skilled in the art will recognize that elements described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with elements described in connection with another. The scope of the invention is defined by the claims that follow.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part of this disclosure and show particular embodiments by way of illustration. Other embodiments may be used and structural or logical changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views.

Overview of the system

FIG. 1 shows a charging control system in which an edge controller 100 manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch. A branch conductor 102 supplies the plurality of connectors from a single point of protection. The allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, referred to in this description as the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors that the branch conductor 102 supplies. The branch limit is a stored value that corresponds to the aggregate current the branch is permitted to carry.

The branch conductor 102 supplies a first connector station 110 and a second connector station 112. Two connector stations are shown for clarity of illustration. The system accommodates a larger plurality of connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each further connector station of the plurality. The branch conductor 102 also supplies a non-charging load 114, which is load connected to the same branch that is not under the control of the edge controller 100.

A branch current sensor 104 measures total current on the branch conductor 102 upstream of the contactors of the connector stations. Because the branch current sensor 104 is located upstream of those contactors, the current it measures includes both the current drawn by the connector stations and the current drawn by the non-charging load 114. The branch current sensor 104 is coupled to the edge controller 100 and reports the measured branch current to it.

The edge controller 100 communicates with the connector stations over an isolated local bus 106. The isolated local bus 106 carries assigned current limits and contactor commands from the edge controller 100 to the connector stations, and carries connector current measurements and control-pilot status from the connector stations to the edge controller 100. The isolated local bus 106 is isolated between the edge controller 100 and the signalling electronics of each connector station.

A network interface 108 connects the edge controller 100 to a remote management system. As described below, the network interface 108 conveys remote schedules and authorizations to the edge controller 100 and conveys uploaded meter records from the edge controller 100, but the safety behaviour of the system does not depend on the availability of the network interface 108.

The connector station

FIG. 2 shows the first connector station 110 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The first connector station 110 comprises a first contactor 120, a first connector current sensor 122, a first control-pilot interface 124, and a first vehicle connector 126. The first contactor 120 is connected in the power path between the branch conductor 102 and the first vehicle connector 126 and, when closed, permits current to flow from the branch conductor 102 to a vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The first connector current sensor 122 measures the connector current flowing in that power path, that is, the current actually drawn by the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126.

The first control-pilot interface 124 presents a control-pilot signal to the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The control-pilot signal advertises a maximum current, called here the assigned limit, that the vehicle is permitted to draw, and reports the state of the coupling, including whether a vehicle is connected. The first control-pilot interface 124 therefore serves both as the command path by which an assigned limit reaches the vehicle and as a status path by which the presence of a connected vehicle is reported to the edge controller 100.

Each connector station of the plurality further has a local connector identifier. The local connector identifier is a stored value that distinguishes one connector of the plurality from another in the records, authorizations, and assignments held by the edge controller 100.

The distinction between the first control-pilot interface 124 and the first connector current sensor 122 is used throughout this description. The first control-pilot interface 124 carries a command. The first connector current sensor 122 carries a measurement. The edge controller 100 does not treat the assigned limit sent through the first control-pilot interface 124 as evidence of the current that the connector is drawing. It obtains that evidence from the first connector current sensor 122.

The edge controller

FIG. 3 shows the edge controller 100 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The edge controller 100 comprises a processing circuit 130 and a nonvolatile memory 132, and is coupled to the isolated local bus 106 and to the network interface 108. The processing circuit 130 executes the allocation and protection processes described below. The nonvolatile memory 132 retains stored values across loss of supply.

The edge controller 100 further comprises a local fault indicator 134 and a service input 136. The local fault indicator 134 provides an indication at the equipment itself, independently of the network interface 108. The service input 136 is an input by which an installer places the edge controller 100 in a commissioning mode.

For each active connector of the plurality, the edge controller 100 stores a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. The charging authorization records that the session at that connector is permitted to draw energy. The requested current is the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained. The minimum sustaining current is the smallest assigned limit at which the session at that connector is expected to remain charging rather than terminating and requiring a new start. The energy-deficit value represents the extent to which the session at that connector has been served less than its requested current over the shared-capacity period. The energy-deficit value increases while a session is held below its request and decreases as the shortfall is made up, and the allocation process described below uses that property of the value.

Allocation at each allocation interval

FIG. 4 shows the process carried out by the edge controller 100. The edge controller 100 repeats the allocation portion of the process at each allocation interval. The allocation interval is a recurring period at which the edge controller 100 revises the assigned limits.

At an available-charging-current determination step 200, the edge controller 100 subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. The measured non-charging branch load is the measured portion of the branch current that is drawn by the non-charging load 114. The configurable safety reserve is a stored margin that is withheld from allocation, so that the branch is not loaded to its limit. Because the non-charging portion of the branch load is measured at each allocation interval and subtracted at the determination step 200, the available charging current follows the varying load of the site, and capacity released by the non-charging load 114 becomes available to the connectors instead of being permanently withheld.

At a minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, the edge controller 100 first assigns the minimum sustaining current to the sessions that can receive it. The minimum sustaining current stored for each session that can receive it is assigned to that session before any further distribution of the available charging current is made.

At a deficit-based distribution step 204, the edge controller 100 distributes the remaining portion of the available charging current, that is, the portion left after the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, according to energy deficit. Sessions with a greater energy-deficit value receive a greater share of the remaining current than sessions with a smaller energy-deficit value. Distributing by energy deficit rather than by instantaneous request corrects, rather than perpetuates, the inequality that arises when one session begins while the branch is heavily loaded and another begins while it is lightly loaded.

At a limit transmission and connector current verification step 206, the edge controller 100 sends each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector, and then verifies the resulting connector current with the connector current sensor of that connector. The allocation is in this way closed loop, using per-connector current sensing together with the independent upstream branch sensing described below.

The branch current sensor as an independent safety input

The branch current sensor 104 is an independent safety input. It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the determination step 200: it governs a protection process that acts on the power path and that does not depend on the cooperation of any vehicle. The protection process is described with continued reference to FIG. 4.

At a pilot reduction step 208, the edge controller 100 compares the measured branch current from the branch current sensor 104 with the branch limit. When the measured branch current is above the branch limit, the edge controller 100 sends a reduced pilot command to at least one connector of the plurality, that is, an assigned limit lower than the limit previously assigned to that connector, and starts a verification interval. The reduced pilot command is the first stage of the response, because reducing current through the control pilot lets a vehicle taper its draw and lets the session continue, which is preferable to interrupting the power path.

At an ordered contactor shedding step 210, the edge controller 100 determines whether the measured branch current remains above the branch limit after the reduced pilot command and after the verification interval has elapsed. The verification interval is long enough for a vehicle that honours the reduced pilot command to have acted on it. If the measured branch current has fallen below the branch limit within the verification interval, the reduced pilot command has been effective and the edge controller 100 returns to the allocation interval process. If the measured branch current remains above the branch limit at the end of the verification interval, the pilot signalling has not produced the required reduction, and the edge controller 100 opens the connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch limit.

The shedding order is a stored value that defines the sequence in which the contactors of the plurality of connector stations are opened. Opening the contactors one at a time, with the measured branch current re-evaluated between openings, removes only as much load as the measurement shows to be necessary: as soon as the measured branch current is below the branch limit, no further contactor is opened, and the remaining sessions continue.

The staged sequence of a reduced pilot command, a verification interval, and then ordered interruption of the power path addresses the technical problem set out in the background. A control-pilot command is advisory, and a vehicle that ignores it, responds too slowly, or responds only in coarse steps leaves the branch loaded above its limit. Allocation that works only from commanded values cannot detect that condition at all. By taking the measured branch current from a sensor that is upstream of every connector contactor, and by treating the persistence of an over-limit measurement through a verification interval as the trigger for opening the power path, the edge controller 100 bounds the branch current with an action that is entirely within its own control, while still giving the cooperative case the opportunity to resolve without interrupting any session.

Recovery after shedding

At a reclose permissive step 212, the edge controller 100 governs the reclosing of a contactor that has been opened by the ordered contactor shedding step 210. The edge controller 100 does not reclose such a contactor until three conditions are satisfied together: the connector current sensor of that connector reports zero current, the control-pilot interface of that connector reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.

Each condition addresses a distinct hazard. A report of zero current from the connector current sensor establishes that the power path is in fact open, so that a reclose command is not issued onto a path that is still carrying current. A report of a connected vehicle from the control-pilot interface establishes that there is a session to restore, so that the power path is not energized to a coupling from which the vehicle has been removed. The randomized recovery delay separates in time the reclosing of the contactors that were shed together, so that the loads do not return in unison and reproduce the overload that the shedding sequence has just relieved.

On reclosing, the edge controller 100 resumes the allocation interval process, and the reclosed session takes part in the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202 and the deficit-based distribution step 204 in the ordinary way.

Welded-contactor isolation

At a welded-contactor isolation step 214, the edge controller 100 records a welded-contactor condition for a connector when the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector. The leakage threshold is a stored current magnitude above zero, so that a connector current that has genuinely ceased is distinguished from a connector current that persists after the open command.

When the welded-contactor condition has been recorded, the edge controller 100 inhibits the other contactors on the same branch and operates the local fault indicator 134. The other contactors are inhibited because a welded contactor consumes branch capacity that neither the allocation process nor the shedding sequence can recover: the shedding sequence believes that opening that contactor has released the current of that connector, and any further allocation made on that belief would overcommit the branch. Inhibiting the other contactors removes the controllable load from the branch and leaves only the current of the welded connector, which is the safe state available to the edge controller 100 with the means at its disposal. The local fault indicator 134 is operated at the equipment because the condition requires physical service and because it must be annunciated whether or not the network interface 108 is available.

Operation during a network outage

The edge controller 100 can receive remote schedules and authorizations through the network interface 108. The edge controller 100 stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in the nonvolatile memory 132. The signed local authorization token identifies the connectors it authorizes by their local connector identifiers and carries an expiry. The last accepted branch limit is the most recent branch limit that the edge controller 100 has accepted from the remote management system.

During a network outage the edge controller 100 continues already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and the independent branch-current safety process described above. Charging therefore continues through the outage within the last accepted branch limit. The edge controller 100 does not start a newly connected session unless the signed local authorization token authorizes that connector and has not expired. A newly connected vehicle at a connector that the token does not authorize, or a newly connected vehicle at any connector after the token has expired, is not started until communication returns and a fresh authorization is obtained.

Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence held locally by the edge controller 100. The records accumulated during the outage are uploaded when communication returns.

Installation mapping through the service input

A multi-connector installation is wired by hand, and the identifier a connector is given in configuration must correspond to the physical contactor and the physical current sensor channel that serve that connector. A transposition assigns a current limit intended for one connector to another. Every component continues to function, every sensor continues to report, and the allocation nevertheless governs the wrong power path.

The service input 136 permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors. With the edge controller 100 in the commissioning mode entered through the service input 136, the edge controller 100 commands one low-energy pilot transition at a time, that is, it drives a pilot transition at a single connector, and confirms the corresponding connector current sensor by observing which sensed channel responds to that transition. The transition is a low-energy one, sufficient to produce a distinguishable response at the connector current sensor of the connector that is actually being driven, and the transitions are commanded one at a time so that the responding channel is unambiguous.

The association between a connector identifier and a physical contactor is stored only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector. If the responding channel is not the channel expected for the commanded connector, or if no channel responds, no association is stored for that connector. The mapping is thus established by measurement on the same sensors that the allocation process later relies upon, so a wiring-map error is found at commissioning instead of silently misdirecting current limits for the life of the installation.

General considerations

The allocation process, the branch protection process, the offline authorization behaviour, the welded-contactor isolation, and the installation mapping are described together because they share the sensors and the isolated local bus 106 of a single edge controller 100. They are nevertheless separable. An embodiment may carry out the allocation and branch protection processes without the offline authorization behaviour, without the tamper-evident record sequence, or without the commissioning mode, and an embodiment may include any combination of those additional features.

The branch limit, the configurable safety reserve, the minimum sustaining current, the shedding order, the leakage threshold, the randomized recovery delay, the length of the allocation interval, and the length of the verification interval are values stored by the edge controller 100.

The terms first and second are used to distinguish one connector station of the plurality from another and do not imply an order of importance or of operation. The system is not limited to two connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each connector station of the plurality. The embodiments described here are illustrative, and a person skilled in the art will recognize that elements described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with elements described in connection with another. The scope of the invention is defined by the claims that follow.

FIG. 1 shows a charging control system in which an edge controller 100 manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch. The allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, referred to in this description as the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors that the branch conductor 102 supplies. The branch conductor 102 supplies a first connector station 110 and a second connector station 112. Two connector stations are shown for clarity of illustration. The system accommodates a larger plurality of connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each further connector station of the plurality. The branch conductor 102 also supplies a non-charging load 114, which is load connected to the same branch that is not under the control of the edge controller 100.

A branch current sensor 104 measures total current on the branch conductor 102 upstream of the contactors of the connector stations. Because the branch current sensor 104 is located upstream of those contactors, the current it measures includes both the current drawn by the connector stations and the current drawn by the non-charging load 114. The branch current sensor 104 is coupled to the edge controller 100 and reports the measured branch current to it.

The edge controller 100 communicates with the connector stations over an isolated local bus 106. The isolated local bus 106 carries assigned current limits and contactor commands from the edge controller 100 to the connector stations, and carries connector current measurements and control-pilot status from the connector stations to the edge controller 100. The isolated local bus 106 is isolated between the edge controller 100 and the connector stations.

A network interface 108 connects the edge controller 100 to a remote management system. As described below, the network interface 108 conveys remote schedules and authorizations to the edge controller 100 and conveys uploaded meter records from the edge controller 100, but the safety behaviour of the system does not depend on the availability of the network interface 108.

The connector station

FIG. 2 shows the first connector station 110 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The first connector station 110 comprises a first contactor 120, a first connector current sensor 122, a first control-pilot interface 124, and a first vehicle connector 126. The first contactor 120 is connected in the power path between the branch conductor 102 and the first vehicle connector 126 and, when closed, permits current to flow from the branch conductor 102 to a vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The first connector current sensor 122 measures the connector current flowing in that power path, that is, the current actually drawn by the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126.

The first control-pilot interface 124 presents a control-pilot signal to the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The control-pilot signal advertises a maximum current, called here the assigned limit, that the vehicle is permitted to draw, and reports the state of the coupling, including whether a vehicle is connected. The first control-pilot interface 124 therefore serves both as the command path by which an assigned limit reaches the vehicle and as a status path by which the presence of a connected vehicle is reported to the edge controller 100.

Each connector station of the plurality further has a local connector identifier. The local connector identifier is a stored value that distinguishes one connector of the plurality from another in the records, authorizations, and assignments held by the edge controller 100.

The distinction between the first control-pilot interface 124 and the first connector current sensor 122 is used throughout this description. The first control-pilot interface 124 carries a command. The first connector current sensor 122 carries a measurement. The edge controller 100 does not treat the assigned limit sent through the first control-pilot interface 124 as evidence of the current that the connector is drawing. It obtains that evidence from the first connector current sensor 122.

The edge controller

FIG. 3 shows the edge controller 100 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The edge controller 100 comprises a processing circuit 130 and a nonvolatile memory 132, and is coupled to the isolated local bus 106 and to the network interface 108. The processing circuit 130 executes the allocation and protection processes described below. The nonvolatile memory 132 retains stored values across loss of supply.

The edge controller 100 further comprises a local fault indicator 134 and a service input 136. The local fault indicator 134 provides an indication at the equipment itself, independently of the network interface 108. The service input 136 is an input by which an installer initiates the association of connector identifiers with physical contactors described below.

For each active connector of the plurality, the edge controller 100 stores a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. The charging authorization records that the session at that connector is permitted to draw energy. The requested current is the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained. The minimum sustaining current is the smallest assigned limit at which the session at that connector is expected to remain charging rather than terminating and requiring a new start. The energy-deficit value represents the extent to which the session at that connector has been served less than its requested current over the shared-capacity period. The energy-deficit value increases while a session is held below its request and decreases as the shortfall is made up, and the allocation process described below uses that property of the value.

Allocation at each allocation interval

FIG. 4 shows the process carried out by the edge controller 100. The edge controller 100 repeats the allocation portion of the process at each allocation interval. The allocation interval is a recurring period at which the edge controller 100 revises the assigned limits.

At an available-charging-current determination step 200, the edge controller 100 subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. The measured non-charging branch load is the measured portion of the branch current that is drawn by the non-charging load 114. The configurable safety reserve is a stored margin that is withheld from allocation, so that the branch is not loaded to its limit. Because the non-charging portion of the branch load is measured at each allocation interval and subtracted at the determination step 200, the available charging current follows the varying load of the site, and capacity released by the non-charging load 114 becomes available to the connectors instead of being permanently withheld.

At a minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, the edge controller 100 first assigns the minimum sustaining current to the sessions that can receive it. The minimum sustaining current stored for each session that can receive it is assigned to that session before any further distribution of the available charging current is made.

At a deficit-based distribution step 204, the edge controller 100 distributes the remaining portion of the available charging current, that is, the portion left after the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, according to energy deficit. Sessions with a greater energy-deficit value receive a greater share of the remaining current than sessions with a smaller energy-deficit value. Distributing by energy deficit rather than by instantaneous request corrects, rather than perpetuates, the inequality that arises when one session begins while the branch is heavily loaded and another begins while it is lightly loaded.

At a limit transmission and connector current verification step 206, the edge controller 100 sends each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector, and then verifies the resulting connector current with the connector current sensor of that connector. The allocation is in this way closed loop, using per-connector current sensing together with the independent upstream branch sensing described below.

The branch current sensor as an independent safety input

The branch current sensor 104 is an independent safety input. It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the determination step 200: it governs a protection process that acts on the power path and that does not depend on the cooperation of any vehicle. The protection process is described with continued reference to FIG. 4.

At a pilot reduction step 208, the edge controller 100 compares the measured branch current from the branch current sensor 104 with the branch limit. When the measured branch current is above the branch limit, the edge controller 100 sends a reduced pilot command to at least one connector of the plurality, that is, an assigned limit lower than the limit previously assigned to that connector, and starts a verification interval. The reduced pilot command is the first stage of the response, because reducing current through the control pilot lets a vehicle taper its draw and lets the session continue, which is preferable to interrupting the power path.

At an ordered contactor shedding step 210, the edge controller 100 determines whether the measured branch current remains above the branch limit after the reduced pilot command and after the verification interval has elapsed. The verification interval is long enough for a vehicle that honours the reduced pilot command to have acted on it. If the measured branch current has fallen below the branch limit within the verification interval, the reduced pilot command has been effective and the edge controller 100 returns to the allocation interval process. If the measured branch current remains above the branch limit at the end of the verification interval, the pilot signalling has not produced the required reduction, and the edge controller 100 opens the connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch limit.

The shedding order is a stored value that defines the sequence in which the contactors of the plurality of connector stations are opened. Opening the contactors one at a time, with the measured branch current re-evaluated between openings, removes only as much load as the measurement shows to be necessary: as soon as the measured branch current is below the branch limit, no further contactor is opened, and the remaining sessions continue.

The staged sequence of a reduced pilot command, a verification interval, and then ordered interruption of the power path addresses the technical problem set out in the background. A control-pilot command is advisory, and a vehicle that ignores it, responds too slowly, or responds only in coarse steps leaves the branch loaded above its limit. Allocation that works only from commanded values cannot detect that condition at all. By taking the measured branch current from a sensor that is upstream of every connector contactor, and by treating the persistence of an over-limit measurement through a verification interval as the trigger for opening the power path, the edge controller 100 bounds the branch current with an action that is entirely within its own control, while still giving the cooperative case the opportunity to resolve without interrupting any session.

Recovery after shedding

At a reclose permissive step 212, the edge controller 100 governs the reclosing of a contactor that has been opened by the ordered contactor shedding step 210. The edge controller 100 does not reclose such a contactor until three conditions are satisfied together: the connector current sensor of that connector reports zero current, the control-pilot interface of that connector reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.

Each condition addresses a distinct hazard. A report of zero current from the connector current sensor establishes that the power path is in fact open, so that a reclose command is not issued onto a path that is still carrying current. A report of a connected vehicle from the control-pilot interface establishes that there is a session to restore, so that the power path is not energized to a coupling from which the vehicle has been removed. The randomized recovery delay separates in time the reclosing of the contactors that were shed together, so that the loads do not return in unison and reproduce the overload that the shedding sequence has just relieved.

On reclosing, the edge controller 100 resumes the allocation interval process, and the reclosed session takes part in the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202 and the deficit-based distribution step 204 in the ordinary way.

At a welded-contactor isolation step 214, the edge controller 100 records a welded-contactor condition for a connector when the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector.
