When the welded-contactor condition has been recorded, the edge controller 100 inhibits the other contactors on the same branch and operates the local fault indicator 134. The other contactors are inhibited because a welded contactor consumes branch capacity that neither the allocation process nor the shedding sequence can recover: the shedding sequence believes that opening that contactor has released the current of that connector, and any further allocation made on that belief would overcommit the branch. Inhibiting the other contactors removes the controllable load from the branch and leaves only the current of the welded connector, which is the safe state available to the edge controller 100 with the means at its disposal. The local fault indicator 134 is operated at the equipment because the condition requires physical service and because it must be annunciated whether or not the network interface 108 is available.

Operation during a network outage

The edge controller 100 can receive remote schedules and authorizations through the network interface 108. The edge controller 100 stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in the nonvolatile memory 132. The signed local authorization token identifies the connectors it authorizes by their local connector identifiers and carries an expiry. The last accepted branch limit is the most recent branch limit that the edge controller 100 has accepted from the remote management system.

During a network outage the edge controller 100 continues already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and the independent branch-current safety process described above. Charging therefore continues through the outage within the last accepted branch limit. The edge controller 100 does not start a newly connected session unless the signed local authorization token authorizes that connector and has not expired. A newly connected vehicle at a connector that the token does not authorize, or a newly connected vehicle at any connector after the token has expired, is not started until communication returns and a fresh authorization is obtained.

Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence held locally by the edge controller 100. The records accumulated during the outage are uploaded when communication returns.

Installation mapping through the service input

A multi-connector installation is wired by hand, and the identifier a connector is given in configuration must correspond to the physical contactor and the physical current sensor channel that serve that connector. A transposition assigns a current limit intended for one connector to another. Every component continues to function, every sensor continues to report, and the allocation nevertheless governs the wrong power path.

The service input 136 permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors. With the edge controller 100 in the commissioning mode entered through the service input 136, the edge controller 100 commands one low-energy pilot transition at a time, that is, it drives a pilot transition at a single connector, and confirms the corresponding connector current sensor by observing which sensed channel responds to that transition. The transition is a low-energy one, sufficient to produce a distinguishable response at the connector current sensor of the connector that is actually being driven, and the transitions are commanded one at a time so that the responding channel is unambiguous.

The association between a connector identifier and a physical contactor is stored only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector. If the responding channel is not the channel expected for the commanded connector, or if no channel responds, no association is stored for that connector. The mapping is thus established by measurement on the same sensors that the allocation process later relies upon, so a wiring-map error is found at commissioning instead of silently misdirecting current limits for the life of the installation.

General considerations

The allocation process, the branch protection process, the offline authorization behaviour, the welded-contactor isolation, and the installation mapping are described together because they share the sensors and the isolated local bus 106 of a single edge controller 100. They are nevertheless separable. An embodiment may carry out the allocation and branch protection processes without the offline authorization behaviour, without the tamper-evident record sequence, or without the commissioning mode, and an embodiment may include any combination of those additional features.

The branch limit, the configurable safety reserve, the minimum sustaining current, the shedding order, the leakage threshold, the randomized recovery delay, the length of the allocation interval, and the length of the verification interval are values stored by the edge controller 100.

The terms first and second are used to distinguish one connector station of the plurality from another and do not imply an order of importance or of operation. The system is not limited to two connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each connector station of the plurality. The embodiments described here are illustrative, and a person skilled in the art will recognize that elements described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with elements described in connection with another. The scope of the invention is defined by the claims that follow.

Overview of the system

FIG. 1 shows a charging control system in which an edge controller 100 manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch. A branch conductor 102 supplies the plurality of connectors from a single point of protection. The allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, referred to in this description as the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors that the branch conductor 102 supplies. The branch limit is a stored value that corresponds to the aggregate current the branch is permitted to carry.

The branch conductor 102 supplies a first connector station 110 and a second connector station 112. Two connector stations are shown for clarity of illustration. The system accommodates a larger plurality of connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each further connector station of the plurality. The branch conductor 102 also supplies a non-charging load 114, which is load connected to the same branch that is not under the control of the edge controller 100.

A branch current sensor 104 measures total current on the branch conductor 102 upstream of the contactors of the connector stations. Because the branch current sensor 104 is located upstream of those contactors, the current it measures includes both the current drawn by the connector stations and the current drawn by the non-charging load 114. The branch current sensor 104 is coupled to the edge controller 100 and reports the measured branch current to it.

The edge controller 100 communicates with the connector stations over an isolated local bus 106. The isolated local bus 106 carries assigned current limits and contactor commands from the edge controller 100 to the connector stations, and carries connector current measurements and control-pilot status from the connector stations to the edge controller 100. The isolated local bus 106 is isolated between the edge controller 100 and the connector stations.

A network interface 108 connects the edge controller 100 to a remote management system. As described below, the network interface 108 conveys remote schedules and authorizations to the edge controller 100 and conveys uploaded meter records from the edge controller 100, but the safety behaviour of the system does not depend on the availability of the network interface 108.

The connector station

FIG. 2 shows the first connector station 110 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The first connector station 110 comprises a first contactor 120, a first connector current sensor 122, a first control-pilot interface 124, and a first vehicle connector 126. The first contactor 120 is connected in the power path between the branch conductor 102 and the first vehicle connector 126 and, when closed, permits current to flow from the branch conductor 102 to a vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The first connector current sensor 122 measures the connector current flowing in that power path, that is, the current actually drawn by the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126.

The first control-pilot interface 124 presents a control-pilot signal to the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The control-pilot signal advertises a maximum current, called here the assigned limit, that the vehicle is permitted to draw, and reports the state of the coupling, including whether a vehicle is connected. The first control-pilot interface 124 therefore serves both as the command path by which an assigned limit reaches the vehicle and as a status path by which the presence of a connected vehicle is reported to the edge controller 100.

Each connector station of the plurality further has a local connector identifier. The local connector identifier is a stored value that distinguishes one connector of the plurality from another in the records, authorizations, and assignments held by the edge controller 100.

The distinction between the first control-pilot interface 124 and the first connector current sensor 122 is used throughout this description. The first control-pilot interface 124 carries a command. The first connector current sensor 122 carries a measurement. The edge controller 100 does not treat the assigned limit sent through the first control-pilot interface 124 as evidence of the current that the connector is drawing. It obtains that evidence from the first connector current sensor 122.

The processing circuit 130 executes the allocation and protection processes described below. The nonvolatile memory 132 retains stored values across loss of supply.

The edge controller 100 further comprises a local fault indicator 134 and a service input 136. The local fault indicator 134 provides an indication at the equipment itself, independently of the network interface 108. The service input 136 is an input by which an installer initiates the association of connector identifiers with physical contactors described below.

For each active connector of the plurality, the edge controller 100 stores a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. The charging authorization records that the session at that connector is permitted to draw energy. The requested current is the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained. The minimum sustaining current is the smallest assigned limit at which the session at that connector is expected to remain charging rather than terminating and requiring a new start. The energy-deficit value represents the extent to which the session at that connector has been served less than its requested current over the shared-capacity period. The energy-deficit value increases while a session is held below its request and decreases as the shortfall is made up, and the allocation process described below uses that property of the value.

Allocation at each allocation interval

FIG. 4 shows the process carried out by the edge controller 100. The edge controller 100 repeats the allocation portion of the process at each allocation interval. The allocation interval is a recurring period at which the edge controller 100 revises the assigned limits.

At an available-charging-current determination step 200, the edge controller 100 subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. The measured non-charging branch load is the measured portion of the branch current that is drawn by the non-charging load 114. The configurable safety reserve is a stored margin that is withheld from allocation, so that the branch is not loaded to its limit. Because the non-charging portion of the branch load is measured at each allocation interval and subtracted at the determination step 200, the available charging current follows the varying load of the site, and capacity released by the non-charging load 114 becomes available to the connectors instead of being permanently withheld.

At a minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, the edge controller 100 first assigns the minimum sustaining current to the sessions that can receive it. The minimum sustaining current stored for each session that can receive it is assigned to that session before any further distribution of the available charging current is made.

At a deficit-based distribution step 204, the edge controller 100 distributes the remaining portion of the available charging current, that is, the portion left after the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, according to energy deficit. Sessions with a greater energy-deficit value receive a greater share of the remaining current than sessions with a smaller energy-deficit value. Distributing by energy deficit rather than by instantaneous request corrects, rather than perpetuates, the inequality that arises when one session begins while the branch is heavily loaded and another begins while it is lightly loaded.

At a limit transmission and connector current verification step 206, the edge controller 100 sends each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector, and then verifies the resulting connector current with the connector current sensor of that connector. The allocation is in this way closed loop, using per-connector current sensing together with the independent upstream branch sensing described below.

The branch current sensor 104 is an independent safety input. It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the determination step 200: it governs a protection process that acts on the power path and that does not depend on the cooperation of any vehicle. The protection process is described with continued reference to FIG. 4.

At a pilot reduction step 208, the edge controller 100 compares the measured branch current from the branch current sensor 104 with the branch limit. When the measured branch current is above the branch limit, the edge controller 100 sends a reduced pilot command to at least one connector of the plurality, that is, an assigned limit lower than the limit previously assigned to that connector, and starts a verification interval. The reduced pilot command is the first stage of the response, because reducing current through the control pilot lets a vehicle taper its draw and lets the session continue, which is preferable to interrupting the power path.

At an ordered contactor shedding step 210, the edge controller 100 determines whether the measured branch current remains above the branch limit after the reduced pilot command and after the verification interval has elapsed. The verification interval is long enough for a vehicle that honours the reduced pilot command to have acted on it. If the measured branch current has fallen below the branch limit within the verification interval, the reduced pilot command has been effective and the edge controller 100 returns to the allocation interval process. If the measured branch current remains above the branch limit at the end of the verification interval, the pilot signalling has not produced the required reduction, and the edge controller 100 opens the connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch limit.

The shedding order is a stored value that defines the sequence in which the contactors of the plurality of connector stations are opened. Opening the contactors one at a time, with the measured branch current re-evaluated between openings, removes only as much load as the measurement shows to be necessary: as soon as the measured branch current is below the branch limit, no further contactor is opened, and the remaining sessions continue.

The staged sequence of a reduced pilot command, a verification interval, and then ordered interruption of the power path addresses the technical problem set out in the background. A control-pilot command is advisory, and a vehicle that ignores it, responds too slowly, or responds only in coarse steps leaves the branch loaded above its limit. Allocation that works only from commanded values cannot detect that condition at all. By taking the measured branch current from a sensor that is upstream of every connector contactor, and by treating the persistence of an over-limit measurement through a verification interval as the trigger for opening the power path, the edge controller 100 bounds the branch current with an action that is entirely within its own control, while still giving the cooperative case the opportunity to resolve without interrupting any session.

Recovery after shedding

At a reclose permissive step 212, the edge controller 100 governs the reclosing of a contactor that has been opened by the ordered contactor shedding step 210. The edge controller 100 does not reclose such a contactor until three conditions are satisfied together: the connector current sensor of that connector reports zero current, the control-pilot interface of that connector reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.

Each condition addresses a distinct hazard. A report of zero current from the connector current sensor establishes that the power path is in fact open, so that a reclose command is not issued onto a path that is still carrying current. A report of a connected vehicle from the control-pilot interface establishes that there is a session to restore, so that the power path is not energized to a coupling from which the vehicle has been removed. The randomized recovery delay separates in time the reclosing of the contactors that were shed together, so that the loads do not return in unison and reproduce the overload that the shedding sequence has just relieved.

On reclosing, the edge controller 100 resumes the allocation interval process, and the reclosed session takes part in the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202 and the deficit-based distribution step 204 in the ordinary way.

send each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector station; and

verify a resulting connector current of that connector station with the connector current sensor of that connector station; and

a branch current sensor arranged to measure a branch current of the electrical branch upstream of the contactors of the plurality of connector stations;

an isolated local bus; and

a controller coupled to the plurality of connector stations over the isolated local bus and coupled to the branch current sensor, the controller configured to store a branch limit that is lower than a sum of ratings of the plurality of electric-vehicle connectors and to store, for each active connector of the plurality of electric-vehicle connectors, a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value;

wherein the controller is configured to, at each allocation interval:

subtract, from the branch limit, a measured non-charging branch load of the electrical branch and a configurable safety reserve, to obtain an available charging current;

assign the minimum sustaining current to those sessions of the active connectors that can receive the minimum sustaining current from the available charging current, and then distribute a remaining portion of the available charging current among the active connectors according to the energy-deficit values;

send each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector station; and

verify a resulting connector current of that connector station with the connector current sensor of that connector station; and

# FIG. 2

View: enlarged schematic block diagram of the first connector station of FIG. 1, drawn in plain line work with no shading. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the filing margins. No text or lettering is drawn by the geometry; the numerals listed below are applied afterward.

Geometry:

- A large plain rectangle encloses the elements of the station. This enclosing rectangle is the first connector station 110, shown schematically.
- A horizontal line enters the enclosing rectangle through its upper left side from a short line at the upper left of the drawing area, that short line being the branch conductor 102, and inside the enclosing rectangle forms the power path running to the right.
- A small open rectangle straddles the power path near the left of the enclosing rectangle, with the power path passing through it. This rectangle is the first contactor 120, shown schematically.
- A second small open rectangle straddles the same power path to the right of the first contactor 120, with the power path passing through it. This rectangle is the first connector current sensor 122, shown schematically.
- The power path ends at the left side of a plain rectangle in the right portion of the enclosing rectangle. This rectangle is the first vehicle connector 126, shown schematically. A short line extends from its right side and terminates inside the drawing area.
- A plain rectangle stands in the lower middle of the enclosing rectangle, below the power path. This rectangle is the first control-pilot interface 124, shown schematically. A line runs from the top side of the first control-pilot interface 124 up to the lower side of the first vehicle connector 126.
- A horizontal line runs along the lower part of the drawing area, below the enclosing rectangle, and rises into it through its lower side, branching inside to the lower side of the first control-pilot interface 124, to the underside of the first connector current sensor 122, and to the underside of the first contactor 120. This connecting line is the isolated local bus 106.

The order of the first contactor 120 and the first connector current sensor 122 along the power path is a drawing convention; both lie in series in the same power path.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part of this disclosure and show particular embodiments by way of illustration. Other embodiments may be used and structural or logical changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views.

Overview of the system

FIG. 1 shows a charging control system in which an edge controller 100 manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch. A branch conductor 102 supplies the plurality of connectors from a single point of protection. The allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, referred to in this description as the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors that the branch conductor 102 supplies. The branch limit is a stored value that corresponds to the aggregate current the branch is permitted to carry.

The branch conductor 102 supplies a first connector station 110 and a second connector station 112. Two connector stations are shown for clarity of illustration. The system accommodates a larger plurality of connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each further connector station of the plurality. The branch conductor 102 also supplies a non-charging load 114, which is load connected to the same branch that is not under the control of the edge controller 100.

A branch current sensor 104 measures total current on the branch conductor 102 upstream of the contactors of the connector stations. Because the branch current sensor 104 is located upstream of those contactors, the current it measures includes both the current drawn by the connector stations and the current drawn by the non-charging load 114. The branch current sensor 104 is coupled to the edge controller 100 and reports the measured branch current to it.

The edge controller 100 communicates with the connector stations over an isolated local bus 106. The isolated local bus 106 carries assigned current limits and contactor commands from the edge controller 100 to the connector stations, and carries connector current measurements and control-pilot status from the connector stations to the edge controller 100. The isolated local bus 106 is isolated between the edge controller 100 and the connector stations.

A network interface 108 connects the edge controller 100 to a remote management system. As described below, the network interface 108 conveys remote schedules and authorizations to the edge controller 100 and conveys uploaded meter records from the edge controller 100, but the safety behaviour of the system does not depend on the availability of the network interface 108.

The connector station

FIG. 2 shows the first connector station 110 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The first connector station 110 comprises a first contactor 120, a first connector current sensor 122, a first control-pilot interface 124, and a first vehicle connector 126. The first contactor 120 is connected in the power path between the branch conductor 102 and the first vehicle connector 126 and, when closed, permits current to flow from the branch conductor 102 to a vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The first connector current sensor 122 measures the connector current flowing in that power path, that is, the current actually drawn by the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126.

The first control-pilot interface 124 presents a control-pilot signal to the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The control-pilot signal advertises a maximum current, called here the assigned limit, that the vehicle is permitted to draw, and reports the state of the coupling, including whether a vehicle is connected. The first control-pilot interface 124 therefore serves both as the command path by which an assigned limit reaches the vehicle and as a status path by which the presence of a connected vehicle is reported to the edge controller 100.

Each connector station of the plurality further has a local connector identifier. The local connector identifier is a stored value that distinguishes one connector of the plurality from another in the records, authorizations, and assignments held by the edge controller 100.

The distinction between the first control-pilot interface 124 and the first connector current sensor 122 is used throughout this description. The first control-pilot interface 124 carries a command. The first connector current sensor 122 carries a measurement. The edge controller 100 does not treat the assigned limit sent through the first control-pilot interface 124 as evidence of the current that the connector is drawing. It obtains that evidence from the first connector current sensor 122.

The edge controller

FIG. 3 shows the edge controller 100 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The edge controller 100 comprises a processing circuit 130 and a nonvolatile memory 132, and is coupled to the isolated local bus 106 and to the network interface 108. The processing circuit 130 executes the allocation and protection processes described below. The nonvolatile memory 132 retains stored values across loss of supply.

The edge controller 100 further comprises a local fault indicator 134 and a service input 136. The local fault indicator 134 provides an indication at the equipment itself, independently of the network interface 108. The service input 136 is an input by which an installer initiates the association of connector identifiers with physical contactors described below.

For each active connector of the plurality, the edge controller 100 stores a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. The charging authorization records that the session at that connector is permitted to draw energy. The requested current is the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained. The minimum sustaining current is the smallest assigned limit at which the session at that connector is expected to remain charging rather than terminating and requiring a new start. The energy-deficit value represents the extent to which the session at that connector has been served less than its requested current over the shared-capacity period. The energy-deficit value increases while a session is held below its request and decreases as the shortfall is made up, and the allocation process described below uses that property of the value.

Allocation at each allocation interval

FIG. 4 shows the process carried out by the edge controller 100. The edge controller 100 repeats the allocation portion of the process at each allocation interval. The allocation interval is a recurring period at which the edge controller 100 revises the assigned limits.

At an available-charging-current determination step 200, the edge controller 100 subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. The measured non-charging branch load is the measured portion of the branch current that is drawn by the non-charging load 114. The configurable safety reserve is a stored margin that is withheld from allocation, so that the branch is not loaded to its limit. Because the non-charging portion of the branch load is measured at each allocation interval and subtracted at the determination step 200, the available charging current follows the varying load of the site, and capacity released by the non-charging load 114 becomes available to the connectors instead of being permanently withheld.

At a minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, the edge controller 100 first assigns the minimum sustaining current to the sessions that can receive it. The minimum sustaining current stored for each session that can receive it is assigned to that session before any further distribution of the available charging current is made.

At a deficit-based distribution step 204, the edge controller 100 distributes the remaining portion of the available charging current, that is, the portion left after the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, according to energy deficit. Sessions with a greater energy-deficit value receive a greater share of the remaining current than sessions with a smaller energy-deficit value. Distributing by energy deficit rather than by instantaneous request corrects, rather than perpetuates, the inequality that arises when one session begins while the branch is heavily loaded and another begins while it is lightly loaded.

At a limit transmission and connector current verification step 206, the edge controller 100 sends each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector, and then verifies the resulting connector current with the connector current sensor of that connector. The allocation is in this way closed loop, using per-connector current sensing together with the independent upstream branch sensing described below.

The branch current sensor as an independent safety input

The branch current sensor 104 is an independent safety input. It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the determination step 200: it governs a protection process that acts on the power path and that does not depend on the cooperation of any vehicle. The protection process is described with continued reference to FIG. 4.

At a pilot reduction step 208, the edge controller 100 compares the measured branch current from the branch current sensor 104 with the branch limit. When the measured branch current is above the branch limit, the edge controller 100 sends a reduced pilot command to at least one connector of the plurality, that is, an assigned limit lower than the limit previously assigned to that connector, and starts a verification interval. The reduced pilot command is the first stage of the response, because reducing current through the control pilot lets a vehicle taper its draw and lets the session continue, which is preferable to interrupting the power path.

At an ordered contactor shedding step 210, the edge controller 100 determines whether the measured branch current remains above the branch limit after the reduced pilot command and after the verification interval has elapsed. The verification interval is long enough for a vehicle that honours the reduced pilot command to have acted on it. The paragraph now says the minimum sustaining current stored for each session that can receive it is assigned before any further distribution is made, which states the order without inventing a sequence among connectors, an exhaustion condition, or an eligibility test. input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged, and the standing caveat applies: prior_art/ holds only an index that lists no references, so nothing is cited and the art behind this draft may be incomplete. This round removed storage-location and mechanism limitations rather than distinguishing features, so what carries claim 1 is what carried it before: the measured upstream branch current governing an action on the power path, namely a reduced pilot command when the measured branch current exceeds the branch limit, a verification interval in which a cooperative vehicle can respond, and then opening the contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current falls below the limit, layered on allocation of an available charging current obtained by subtracting a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve, with the minimum sustaining current assigned first, the remainder distributed by energy deficit, and each assigned limit verified at the connector current sensor. In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part of this disclosure and show particular embodiments by way of illustration. Other embodiments may be used and structural or logical changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views.

Overview of the system

FIG. 1 shows a charging control system in which an edge controller 100 manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch. A branch conductor 102 supplies the plurality of connectors from a single point of protection. The allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, referred to in this description as the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors that the branch conductor 102 supplies. The branch limit is a stored value that corresponds to the aggregate current the branch is permitted to carry.

The branch conductor 102 supplies a first connector station 110 and a second connector station 112. Two connector stations are shown for clarity of illustration. The system accommodates a larger plurality of connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each further connector station of the plurality. The branch conductor 102 also supplies a non-charging load 114, which is load connected to the same branch that is not under the control of the edge controller 100.

A branch current sensor 104 measures total current on the branch conductor 102 upstream of the contactors of the connector stations. Because the branch current sensor 104 is located upstream of those contactors, the current it measures includes both the current drawn by the connector stations and the current drawn by the non-charging load 114. The branch current sensor 104 is coupled to the edge controller 100 and reports the measured branch current to it.

The edge controller 100 communicates with the connector stations over an isolated local bus 106. The isolated local bus 106 carries assigned current limits and contactor commands from the edge controller 100 to the connector stations, and carries connector current measurements and control-pilot status from the connector stations to the edge controller 100. The isolated local bus 106 is isolated between the edge controller 100 and the connector stations.

A network interface 108 connects the edge controller 100 to a remote management system. As described below, the network interface 108 conveys remote schedules and authorizations to the edge controller 100 and conveys uploaded meter records from the edge controller 100, but the safety behaviour of the system does not depend on the availability of the network interface 108.

The connector station

FIG. 2 shows the first connector station 110 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The first connector station 110 comprises a first contactor 120, a first connector current sensor 122, a first control-pilot interface 124, and a first vehicle connector 126. The first contactor 120 is connected in the power path between the branch conductor 102 and the first vehicle connector 126 and, when closed, permits current to flow from the branch conductor 102 to a vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The first connector current sensor 122 measures the connector current flowing in that power path, that is, the current actually drawn by the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126.

The first control-pilot interface 124 presents a control-pilot signal to the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The control-pilot signal advertises a maximum current, called here the assigned limit, that the vehicle is permitted to draw, and reports the state of the coupling, including whether a vehicle is connected. The first control-pilot interface 124 therefore serves both as the command path by which an assigned limit reaches the vehicle and as a status path by which the presence of a connected vehicle is reported to the edge controller 100.

Each connector station of the plurality further has a local connector identifier. The local connector identifier is a stored value that distinguishes one connector of the plurality from another in the records, authorizations, and assignments held by the edge controller 100.

The distinction between the first control-pilot interface 124 and the first connector current sensor 122 is used throughout this description. The first control-pilot interface 124 carries a command. The first connector current sensor 122 carries a measurement. The edge controller 100 does not treat the assigned limit sent through the first control-pilot interface 124 as evidence of the current that the connector is drawing. It obtains that evidence from the first connector current sensor 122.

The edge controller

FIG. 3 shows the edge controller 100 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The edge controller 100 comprises a processing circuit 130 and a nonvolatile memory 132, and is coupled to the isolated local bus 106 and to the network interface 108. The processing circuit 130 executes the allocation and protection processes described below. The nonvolatile memory 132 retains stored values across loss of supply.

The edge controller 100 further comprises a local fault indicator 134 and a service input 136. The local fault indicator 134 provides an indication at the equipment itself, independently of the network interface 108. The service input 136 is an input by which an installer initiates the association of connector identifiers with physical contactors described below.

For each active connector of the plurality, the edge controller 100 stores a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. The charging authorization records that the session at that connector is permitted to draw energy. The requested current is the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained. The minimum sustaining current is the smallest assigned limit at which the session at that connector is expected to remain charging rather than terminating and requiring a new start. The energy-deficit value represents the extent to which the session at that connector has been served less than its requested current over the shared-capacity period. The energy-deficit value increases while a session is held below its request and decreases as the shortfall is made up, and the allocation process described below uses that property of the value.

Allocation at each allocation interval

FIG. 4 shows the process carried out by the edge controller 100. The edge controller 100 repeats the allocation portion of the process at each allocation interval. The allocation interval is a recurring period at which the edge controller 100 revises the assigned limits.

At an available-charging-current determination step 200, the edge controller 100 subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. The measured non-charging branch load is the measured portion of the branch current that is drawn by the non-charging load 114. The configurable safety reserve is a stored margin that is withheld from allocation, so that the branch is not loaded to its limit. Because the non-charging portion of the branch load is measured at each allocation interval and subtracted at the determination step 200, the available charging current follows the varying load of the site, and capacity released by the non-charging load 114 becomes available to the connectors instead of being permanently withheld.

At a minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, the edge controller 100 first assigns the minimum sustaining current to the sessions that can receive it. The minimum sustaining current stored for each such session is assigned to that session before any further distribution of the available charging current is made.

At a deficit-based distribution step 204, the edge controller 100 distributes the remaining portion of the available charging current, that is, the portion left after the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, according to energy deficit. Sessions with a greater energy-deficit value receive a greater share of the remaining current than sessions with a smaller energy-deficit value. Distributing by energy deficit rather than by instantaneous request corrects, rather than perpetuates, the inequality that arises when one session begins while the branch is heavily loaded and another begins while it is lightly loaded.

At a limit transmission and connector current verification step 206, the edge controller 100 sends each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector, and then verifies the resulting connector current with the connector current sensor of that connector. The allocation is in this way closed loop, using per-connector current sensing together with the independent upstream branch sensing described below.

The branch current sensor as an independent safety input

The branch current sensor 104 is an independent safety input. It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the determination step 200: it governs a protection process that acts on the power path and that does not depend on the cooperation of any vehicle. The protection process is described with continued reference to FIG. 4.

At a pilot reduction step 208, the edge controller 100 compares the measured branch current from the branch current sensor 104 with the branch limit. When the measured branch current is above the branch limit, the edge controller 100 sends a reduced pilot command to at least one connector of the plurality, that is, an assigned limit lower than the limit previously assigned to that connector, and starts a verification interval. The reduced pilot command is the first stage of the response, because reducing current through the control pilot lets a vehicle taper its draw and lets the session continue, which is preferable to interrupting the power path.

At an ordered contactor shedding step 210, the edge controller 100 determines whether the measured branch current remains above the branch limit after the reduced pilot command and after the verification interval has elapsed. The verification interval is long enough for a vehicle that honours the reduced pilot command to have acted on it. If the measured branch current has fallen below the branch limit within the verification interval, the reduced pilot command has been effective and the edge controller 100 returns to the allocation interval process. If the measured branch current remains above the branch limit at the end of the verification interval, the pilot signalling has not produced the required reduction, and the edge controller 100 opens the connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch limit.

The shedding order is a stored value that defines the sequence in which the contactors of the plurality of connector stations are opened. Opening the contactors one at a time, with the measured branch current re-evaluated between openings, removes only as much load as the measurement shows to be necessary: as soon as the measured branch current is below the branch limit, no further contactor is opened, and the remaining sessions continue.

The staged sequence of a reduced pilot command, a verification interval, and then ordered interruption of the power path addresses the technical problem set out in the background. A control-pilot command is advisory, and a vehicle that ignores it, responds too slowly, or responds only in coarse steps leaves the branch loaded above its limit. Allocation that works only from commanded values cannot detect that condition at all. By taking the measured branch current from a sensor that is upstream of every connector contactor, and by treating the persistence of an over-limit measurement through a verification interval as the trigger for opening the power path, the edge controller 100 bounds the branch current with an action that is entirely within its own control, while still giving the cooperative case the opportunity to resolve without interrupting any session.

Recovery after shedding

At a reclose permissive step 212, the edge controller 100 governs the reclosing of a contactor that has been opened by the ordered contactor shedding step 210. The edge controller 100 does not reclose such a contactor until three conditions are satisfied together: the connector current sensor of that connector reports zero current, the control-pilot interface of that connector reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.

Each condition addresses a distinct hazard. A report of zero current from the connector current sensor establishes that the power path is in fact open, so that a reclose command is not issued onto a path that is still carrying current. A report of a connected vehicle from the control-pilot interface establishes that there is a session to restore, so that the power path is not energized to a coupling from which the vehicle has been removed. The randomized recovery delay separates in time the reclosing of the contactors that were shed together, so that the loads do not return in unison and reproduce the overload that the shedding sequence has just relieved.

On reclosing, the edge controller 100 resumes the allocation interval process, and the reclosed session takes part in the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202 and the deficit-based distribution step 204 in the ordinary way.

Welded-contactor isolation

At a welded-contactor isolation step 214, the edge controller 100 records a welded-contactor condition for a connector when the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector. The leakage threshold is a stored current magnitude above zero, so that a connector current that has genuinely ceased is distinguished from a connector current that persists after the open command.

When the welded-contactor condition has been recorded, the edge controller 100 inhibits the other contactors on the same branch and operates the local fault indicator 134. The other contactors are inhibited because a welded contactor consumes branch capacity that neither the allocation process nor the shedding sequence can recover: the shedding sequence believes that opening that contactor has released the current of that connector, and any further allocation made on that belief would overcommit the branch. Inhibiting the other contactors removes the controllable load from the branch and leaves only the current of the welded connector, which is the safe state available to the edge controller 100 with the means at its disposal. The local fault indicator 134 is operated at the equipment because the condition requires physical service and because it must be annunciated whether or not the network interface 108 is available.

Operation during a network outage

The edge controller 100 can receive remote schedules and authorizations through the network interface 108. The edge controller 100 stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in the nonvolatile memory 132. The signed local authorization token authorizes one or more connectors of the plurality and has an expiry. The last accepted branch limit is the most recent branch limit that the edge controller 100 has accepted from the remote management system.

During a network outage the edge controller 100 continues already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and the independent branch-current safety process described above. Charging therefore continues through the outage within the last accepted branch limit. The edge controller 100 does not start a newly connected session unless the signed local authorization token authorizes that connector and has not expired. A newly connected vehicle at a connector that the token does not authorize, or a newly connected vehicle at any connector after the token has expired, is not started until communication returns and a fresh authorization is obtained.

Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence held locally by the edge controller 100. The records accumulated during the outage are uploaded when communication returns.

Installation mapping through the service input

A multi-connector installation is wired by hand, and the identifier a connector is given in configuration must correspond to the physical contactor and the physical current sensor channel that serve that connector. A transposition assigns a current limit intended for one connector to another. Every component continues to function, every sensor continues to report, and the allocation nevertheless governs the wrong power path.

The service input 136 permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors. In response to the service input 136, the edge controller 100 commands one low-energy pilot transition at a time, that is, it drives a pilot transition at a single connector, and confirms the corresponding connector current sensor by observing which sensed channel responds to that transition. The transition is a low-energy one, sufficient to produce a distinguishable response at the connector current sensor of the connector that is actually being driven, and the transitions are commanded one at a time so that the responding channel is unambiguous.

The association between a connector identifier and a physical contactor is stored only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector. If the responding channel is not the channel expected for the commanded connector, or if no channel responds, no association is stored for that connector. The mapping is thus established by measurement on the same sensors that the allocation process later relies upon, so a wiring-map error is found during installation instead of silently misdirecting current limits for the life of the installation.

General considerations

The allocation process, the branch protection process, the offline authorization behaviour, the welded-contactor isolation, and the installation mapping are described together because they share the sensors and the isolated local bus 106 of a single edge controller 100. They are nevertheless separable. An embodiment may carry out the allocation and branch protection processes without the offline authorization behaviour, without the tamper-evident record sequence, or without the installation mapping described above, and an embodiment may include any combination of those additional features.

The branch limit, the configurable safety reserve, the minimum sustaining current, the shedding order, the leakage threshold, the randomized recovery delay, the length of the allocation interval, and the length of the verification interval are values stored by the edge controller 100.

The terms first and second are used to distinguish one connector station of the plurality from another and do not imply an order of importance or of operation. The system is not limited to two connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each connector station of the plurality. The embodiments described here are illustrative, and a person skilled in the art will recognize that elements described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with elements described in connection with another. The scope of the invention is defined by the claims that follow.

The branch current sensor 104 is coupled to the edge controller 100 and reports the measured branch current to it.

The edge controller 100 communicates with the connector stations over an isolated local bus 106. The isolated local bus 106 carries assigned current limits and contactor commands from the edge controller 100 to the connector stations, and carries connector current measurements and control-pilot status from the connector stations to the edge controller 100. The isolated local bus 106 is isolated between the edge controller 100 and the connector stations.

A network interface 108 connects the edge controller 100 to a remote management system. As described below, the network interface 108 conveys remote schedules and authorizations to the edge controller 100 and conveys uploaded meter records from the edge controller 100, but the safety behaviour of the system does not depend on the availability of the network interface 108.

The connector station

FIG. 2 shows the first connector station 110 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The first connector station 110 comprises a first contactor 120, a first connector current sensor 122, a first control-pilot interface 124, and a first vehicle connector 126. The first contactor 120 is connected in the power path between the branch conductor 102 and the first vehicle connector 126 and, when closed, permits current to flow from the branch conductor 102 to a vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The first connector current sensor 122 measures the connector current flowing in that power path, that is, the current actually drawn by the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126.

The first control-pilot interface 124 presents a control-pilot signal to the vehicle coupled to the first vehicle connector 126. The control-pilot signal advertises a maximum current, called here the assigned limit, that the vehicle is permitted to draw, and reports the state of the coupling, including whether a vehicle is connected. The first control-pilot interface 124 therefore serves both as the command path by which an assigned limit reaches the vehicle and as a status path by which the presence of a connected vehicle is reported to the edge controller 100.

Each connector station of the plurality further has a local connector identifier. The local connector identifier is a stored value that distinguishes one connector of the plurality from another in the records, authorizations, and assignments held by the edge controller 100.

The distinction between the first control-pilot interface 124 and the first connector current sensor 122 is used throughout this description. The first control-pilot interface 124 carries a command. The first connector current sensor 122 carries a measurement. The edge controller 100 does not treat the assigned limit sent through the first control-pilot interface 124 as evidence of the current that the connector is drawing. It obtains that evidence from the first connector current sensor 122.

The edge controller

FIG. 3 shows the edge controller 100 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The edge controller 100 comprises a processing circuit 130 and a nonvolatile memory 132, and is coupled to the isolated local bus 106 and to the network interface 108. The processing circuit 130 executes the allocation and protection processes described below. The nonvolatile memory 132 retains stored values across loss of supply.

The edge controller 100 further comprises a local fault indicator 134 and a service input 136. The local fault indicator 134 provides an indication at the equipment itself, independently of the network interface 108. The service input 136 is an input by which an installer initiates the association of connector identifiers with physical contactors described below.

For each active connector of the plurality, the edge controller 100 stores a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. The charging authorization records that the session at that connector is permitted to draw energy. The requested current is the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained. The minimum sustaining current is the smallest assigned limit at which the session at that connector is expected to remain charging rather than terminating and requiring a new start. The energy-deficit value represents the extent to which the session at that connector has been served less than its requested current over the shared-capacity period. The energy-deficit value increases while a session is held below its request and decreases as the shortfall is made up, and the allocation process described below uses that property of the value.

Allocation at each allocation interval

FIG. 4 shows the process carried out by the edge controller 100. The edge controller 100 repeats the allocation portion of the process at each allocation interval. The allocation interval is a recurring period at which the edge controller 100 revises the assigned limits.

At an available-charging-current determination step 200, the edge controller 100 subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. The measured non-charging branch load is the measured portion of the branch current that is drawn by the non-charging load 114. The configurable safety reserve is a stored margin that is withheld from allocation, so that the branch is not loaded to its limit. Because the non-charging portion of the branch load is measured at each allocation interval and subtracted at the determination step 200, the available charging current follows the varying load of the site, and capacity released by the non-charging load 114 becomes available to the connectors instead of being permanently withheld.

At a minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, the edge controller 100 first assigns the minimum sustaining current to the sessions that can receive it. The minimum sustaining current stored for each such session is assigned to that session before any further distribution of the available charging current is made.

At a deficit-based distribution step 204, the edge controller 100 distributes the remaining portion of the available charging current, that is, the portion left after the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, according to energy deficit. Sessions with a greater energy-deficit value receive a greater share of the remaining current than sessions with a smaller energy-deficit value. Distributing by energy deficit rather than by instantaneous request corrects, rather than perpetuates, the inequality that arises when one session begins while the branch is heavily loaded and another begins while it is lightly loaded.

At a limit transmission and connector current verification step 206, the edge controller 100 sends each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector, and then verifies the resulting connector current with the connector current sensor of that connector. The allocation is in this way closed loop, using per-connector current sensing together with the independent upstream branch sensing described below.

The branch current sensor as an independent safety input

The branch current sensor 104 is an independent safety input. It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the determination step 200: it governs a protection process that acts on the power path and that does not depend on the cooperation of any vehicle. The protection process is described with continued reference to FIG. 4.

At a pilot reduction step 208, the edge controller 100 compares the measured branch current from the branch current sensor 104 with the branch limit. When the measured branch current is above the branch limit, the edge controller 100 sends a reduced pilot command to at least one connector of the plurality, that is, an assigned limit lower than the limit previously assigned to that connector, and starts a verification interval. The reduced pilot command is the first stage of the response, because reducing current through the control pilot lets a vehicle taper its draw and lets the session continue, which is preferable to interrupting the power path.

At an ordered contactor shedding step 210, the edge controller 100 determines whether the measured branch current remains above the branch limit after the reduced pilot command and after the verification interval has elapsed. The verification interval is long enough for a vehicle that honours the reduced pilot command to have acted on it. If the measured branch current has fallen below the branch limit within the verification interval, the reduced pilot command has been effective and the edge controller 100 returns to the allocation interval process. If the measured branch current remains above the branch limit at the end of the verification interval, the pilot signalling has not produced the required reduction, and the edge controller 100 opens the connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch limit.

The shedding order is a stored value that defines the sequence in which the contactors of the plurality of connector stations are opened. Opening the contactors one at a time, with the measured branch current re-evaluated between openings, removes only as much load as the measurement shows to be necessary: as soon as the measured branch current is below the branch limit, no further contactor is opened, and the remaining sessions continue.

The staged sequence of a reduced pilot command, a verification interval, and then ordered interruption of the power path addresses the technical problem set out in the background. A control-pilot command is advisory, and a vehicle that ignores it, responds too slowly, or responds only in coarse steps leaves the branch loaded above its limit. Allocation that works only from commanded values cannot detect that condition at all. By taking the measured branch current from a sensor that is upstream of every connector contactor, and by treating the persistence of an over-limit measurement through a verification interval as the trigger for opening the power path, the edge controller 100 bounds the branch current with an action that is entirely within its own control, while still giving the cooperative case the opportunity to resolve without interrupting any session.

Recovery after shedding

At a reclose permissive step 212, the edge controller 100 governs the reclosing of a contactor that has been opened by the ordered contactor shedding step 210. The edge controller 100 does not reclose such a contactor until three conditions are satisfied together: the connector current sensor of that connector reports zero current, the control-pilot interface of that connector reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.

Each condition addresses a distinct hazard. A report of zero current from the connector current sensor establishes that the power path is in fact open, so that a reclose command is not issued onto a path that is still carrying current. A report of a connected vehicle from the control-pilot interface establishes that there is a session to restore, so that the power path is not energized to a coupling from which the vehicle has been removed. The randomized recovery delay separates in time the reclosing of the contactors that were shed together, so that the loads do not return in unison and reproduce the overload that the shedding sequence has just relieved.

On reclosing, the edge controller 100 resumes the allocation interval process, and the reclosed session takes part in the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202 and the deficit-based distribution step 204 in the ordinary way.

Welded-contactor isolation

At a welded-contactor isolation step 214, the edge controller 100 records a welded-contactor condition for a connector when the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector. The leakage threshold is a stored current magnitude above zero, so that a connector current that has genuinely ceased is distinguished from a connector current that persists after the open command.

When the welded-contactor condition has been recorded, the edge controller 100 inhibits the other contactors on the same branch and operates the local fault indicator 134. The other contactors are inhibited because a welded contactor consumes branch capacity that neither the allocation process nor the shedding sequence can recover: the shedding sequence believes that opening that contactor has released the current of that connector, and any further allocation made on that belief would overcommit the branch. Inhibiting the other contactors prevents further controllable load from being placed on the branch while the welded contactor continues to conduct. The local fault indicator 134 is operated at the equipment because the condition requires physical service and because it must be annunciated whether or not the network interface 108 is available.

Operation during a network outage

The edge controller 100 can receive remote schedules and authorizations through the network interface 108. The edge controller 100 stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in the nonvolatile memory 132. The signed local authorization token authorizes one or more connectors of the plurality and has an expiry. The last accepted branch limit is the most recent branch limit that the edge controller 100 has accepted from the remote management system.

During a network outage the edge controller 100 continues already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and the independent branch-current safety process described above. Charging therefore continues through the outage within the last accepted branch limit. The edge controller 100 does not start a newly connected session unless the signed local authorization token authorizes that connector and has not expired. A newly connected vehicle at a connector that the token does not authorize, or a newly connected vehicle at any connector after the token has expired, is not started until communication returns and a fresh authorization is obtained.

Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence held locally by the edge controller 100. The records accumulated during the outage are uploaded when communication returns.

Installation mapping through the service input

A multi-connector installation is wired by hand, and the identifier a connector is given in configuration must correspond to the physical contactor and the physical current sensor channel that serve that connector. A transposition assigns a current limit intended for one connector to another. Every component continues to function, every sensor continues to report, and the allocation nevertheless governs the wrong power path.

The service input 136 permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors. In response to the service input 136, the edge controller 100 commands one low-energy pilot transition at a time, that is, it drives a pilot transition at a single connector, and confirms the corresponding connector current sensor by observing which sensed channel responds to that transition. The transition is a low-energy one, sufficient to produce a distinguishable response at the connector current sensor of the connector that is actually being driven, and the transitions are commanded one at a time so that the responding channel is unambiguous.

The association between a connector identifier and a physical contactor is stored only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector. If the responding channel is not the channel expected for the commanded connector, or if no channel responds, no association is stored for that connector. The mapping is thus established by measurement on the same sensors that the allocation process later relies upon, so a wiring-map error is found during installation instead of silently misdirecting current limits for the life of the installation.

General considerations

The allocation process, the branch protection process, the offline authorization behaviour, the welded-contactor isolation, and the installation mapping are described together because they share the sensors and the isolated local bus 106 of a single edge controller 100. They are nevertheless separable. An embodiment may carry out the allocation and branch protection processes without the offline authorization behaviour, without the tamper-evident record sequence, or without the installation mapping described above, and an embodiment may include any combination of those additional features.

The branch limit, the configurable safety reserve, the minimum sustaining current, the shedding order, the leakage threshold, the randomized recovery delay, the length of the allocation interval, and the length of the verification interval are values stored by the edge controller 100.

The terms first and second are used to distinguish one connector station of the plurality from another and do not imply an order of importance or of operation. The system is not limited to two connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each connector station of the plurality. The embodiments described here are illustrative, and a person skilled in the art will recognize that elements described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with elements described in connection with another. The scope of the invention is defined by the claims that follow.

A branch conductor 102 supplies the plurality of connectors from a single point of protection. Both findings are fixed, and nothing else needed to move.

**Welded-contactor paragraph**: the sentence asserting that inhibition removes controllable load and leaves only the welded connector's current now reads "Inhibiting the other contactors prevents further controllable load from being placed on the branch while the welded contactor continues to conduct." That matches the neutral verb already used in claims 4 and 11, so no claim amendment was needed.

**Overview paragraph**: "from a single point of protection" deleted; the sentence now reads "A branch conductor 102 supplies the plurality of connectors." No other text depended on the phrase, and no claim recites it.

Verified after the edits: no leftover instances of either phrase anywhere in `draft/`; all 24 numerals still one-to-one across the description, `numerals.md`, and the four figure briefs; figure briefs unchanged at 2768, 2717, 2784, and 2764 characters; abstract unchanged at 142 words (146 with hyphens split); 14 claims intact; no placeholders, notes, or em dashes.

input.summary: Fixed both findings, each confined to the detailed description. The welded-contactor paragraph no longer asserts that inhibiting the other contactors removes existing load or leaves the branch carrying only the welded connector's current; it now states only that inhibition prevents further controllable load from being placed on the branch while the welded contactor continues to conduct, which matches the neutral verb already used in claims 4 and 11. The phrase "from a single point of protection" is deleted from the system overview, since the disclosure never describes a protective device or point of protection and the only such mention elsewhere is Background prior-art framing. No claim, numeral, figure brief, or other section required a change, and I verified that rather than assuming it.
reasoning: Both findings were about the description asserting more than the inventor said, so both were fixed by narrowing the prose to what the source states, not by adjusting claims. The disclosure stops at 'inhibits the other contactors on the same branch', so the description now stops there too: inhibition prevents further controllable load from being placed on the branch. It no longer characterizes the resulting branch state.

Claims 4 and 11 already recited inhibition in neutral terms, so leaving them untouched was the right call; amending them would have introduced a mismatch where none existed. The fix restores agreement between the description's explanation and the claims' language.

The point-of-protection phrase carried no claim weight, since claims 1 and 9 recite only a common electrical branch and a stored branch limit, so deleting it costs no scope. I checked that nothing downstream in the description depended on it before removing it, and the surrounding sentences about the branch limit still read as a complete definition.

The Background's reference to a branch protective device stays as written. It is prior-art framing of the problem rather than invention text, and the review scoped Background characterizations out of the source-fidelity trace.

After editing I re-ran the full consistency pass rather than assuming the small edits were isolated: no leftover instances of either phrase, all 24 numerals still one-to-one across description, numeral table, and figure briefs, figure briefs unchanged and within the length cap, abstract unchanged at 142 words, and 14 claims intact.

draft/08-detailed-description.md:27:FIG. 3 shows the edge controller 100 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The edge controller 100 comprises a processing circuit 130 and a nonvolatile memory 132, and is coupled to the isolated local bus 106 and to the network interface 108. The processing circuit 130 executes the allocation and protection processes described below. The nonvolatile memory 132 retains stored values across loss of supply.
draft/08-detailed-description.md:31:For each active connector of the plurality, the edge controller 100 stores a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. The charging authorization records that the session at that connector is permitted to draw energy. The requested current is the current that the session would take if capacity were unconstrained. The minimum sustaining current is the smallest assigned limit at which the session at that connector is expected to remain charging rather than terminating and requiring a new start. The energy-deficit value represents the extent to which the session at that connector has been served less than its requested current over the shared-capacity period. The energy-deficit value increases while a session is held below its request and decreases as the shortfall is made up, and the allocation process described below uses that property of the value.
draft/06-summary.md:5:The controller stores, for each active connector, a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. At each allocation interval the controller subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. It first assigns the minimum sustaining current to the sessions that can receive it, and then distributes the remaining portion of the available charging current according to energy deficit, so that a session that has been served less over the shared-capacity period is preferred over a session that has been served more. Each assigned limit is sent through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector, and the resulting connector current is then verified with the connector current sensor of that same connector. Allocation is therefore closed loop, using per-connector current sensing together with independent upstream branch sensing.
draft/05-background.md:7:Sharing schemes that divide available current equally, or in proportion to instantaneous request, also tend to treat every session alike. Where sessions have been served unequally over the course of a shared-capacity period, for example because one session began while the branch was heavily loaded and another began while it was lightly loaded, equal division perpetuates the inequality rather than correcting it.
